Robotics.comment: 45 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables. Structured narrative review of hardware, data, cross-embodiment transfer, foundation models, tactile sensing, and evaluation for dexterous robotic hands

Robotics.title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
Robotics.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.

Robotics.title: When to Ask for Help: Uncertainty-Triggered Aerial Refinement for Off-Road Navigation
Robotics.summary: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

Robotics.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Effects of Haptic Feedback for ROV Teleoperation in Hazardous Environments
Robotics.summary:
Teleoperating a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in complex underwater environments presents unique challenges. Dynamic, three dimensional obstacles and unseen water currents pose real risks to expensive robotic hardware in environments in which recovery can be next to impossible. This paper explores the cognitive effects of haptic feedback to improve vehicle safety in such environments. An in-water study is analysed with a ROV exposed to controlled cross-currents, with environmental information presented via a soft and vibrating haptic touchpad.
  Results demonstrate that while encountering an unseen cross-current significantly increases an operator's physical and temporal demand, the introduction of haptic feedback mitigates these factors and improves self-assessed performance. Interestingly, the haptic condition also produced the highest levels of mental demand and operator frustration. Despite this increased mental workload, operators drove the ROV significantly faster when receiving haptic cues compared to the current-only condition, indicating a higher level of user confidence. Ultimately, these findings suggest that while haptic feedback may initially require more cognitive processing to interpret unseen hazards, it successfully enhances operator awareness and promotes more confident navigation in hazardous environments.

Robotics.title: Which Physical Tactile Cues Matter for Contact-Rich Imitation Learning? A Controlled Real-Robot Study
Robotics.summary: Vision-based tactile sensors capture multiple aspects of physical interaction within a single image stream, including contact appearance, geometry, indentation depth, and tangential deformation. However, existing visuo-tactile policies often directly process tactile observations as images, making it difficult to determine which physical cues contribute to policy learning. This paper presents a controlled real-robot study that compares physically interpretable tactile signals using the LeRobot platform, enhanced with our visuo-tactile perception system. From the same tactile stream, we derive tactile RGB images, normal/depth maps, and marker-flow fields, representing contact appearance, geometry, and tangential deformation, respectively. Using identical task demonstrations and the same policy backbone, we evaluate the individual and combined contributions of these tactile cues. We further compare tactile encoders and visuo-tactile fusion strategies. Evaluation across 720 real-robot trials yields four key findings: (1) tactile perception substantially improves the overall success rate from 57.8% to 78.9%, although its contribution varies across task stages; (2) marker flow is the most effective individual cue, achieving a success rate of 74.4% and playing a particularly important role in regulating established contact; (3) cue-factorized encoding consistently improves performance, highlighting that different physical cues require tailored processing techniques; and (4) although the effectiveness of tactile fusion is task-dependent, cross-attention offers a lightweight solution with performance comparable to that of pretrained tactile encoders.
Robotics.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to IEEE ROBIO 2026

Robotics.title: SUPER - Sensitivity-based Uncertainty-aware Performance and Risk Assessment in Visual Inertial Odometry
Robotics.summary: This paper presents SUPER (Sensitivity-based Uncertainty-aware PErformance and Risk assessment), a bounded controller that adapts visual measurement information in visual-inertial odometry at runtime. Building on multi-view landmark dispersion from stereo observations, SUPER projects track consistency into pixel space and combines it with the reprojection residual to gate a temporally smoothed, bounded information update. Because the controller operates inside nondeterministic optimizers, we additionally propose an action-verification protocol based on factor-level logs, inactive-instrumented controls, and same-linearization replay. We evaluate SUPER in Ceres and g2o backends on EuRoC, TUM-VI, UMA-VI, and TartanAir under controlled visual corruptions, with a frozen policy and prospective confirmation. SUPER is computationally efficient and selectively active, but does not establish a general accuracy improvement: all 13 split-level confidence intervals cross zero, and effects are heterogeneous across corruption families. The action-verification protocol reliably distinguishes controller-induced state changes from solver variability.
Robotics.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. v2: substantially revised. The Schur-complement risk indicator of v1 is replaced by a closed-loop controller adapting visual information from multi-view track dispersion, with a new action-verification protocol. ISO risk mapping and the prediction/stop-policy results of v1 are removed. v2 claims no general accuracy improvement

Robotics.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics
Robotics.summary: Flapping-wing simulation need to reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation. The source code are available at: https://mingshanhe.github.io/FlapSim/\href{https://mingshanhe.github.io/FlapSim/}.

Robotics.title: Compounding Physical RSI: Turning Execution Failure into Inherited Capability
Robotics.summary:
Generalist robot policies are trained on static offline datasets, yet physical manipulation unfolds sequentially across stages. Because a weakness in a downstream stage remains unobservable until the policy passes earlier ones, each resolved bottleneck exposes the next hidden failure mode. This staged structure calls for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), in which a policy iteratively executes, diagnoses failures, and updates itself. Moreover, because task completion behaves like a product of stage-level pass rates, recursive gains can multiply across generations. In physical environments, three bottlenecks obstruct compounding: terminal execution feedback rarely localizes the stage that caused a failure, failed trajectories do not supply the corrective action, and updating shared parameters can degrade previously mastered skills.
  We propose Compounding Physical RSI, a self-evolving policy framework that turns execution failures into heritable capability. First, automated capability-gap assessment traces failed rollouts to the task stage where progression breaks down and formulates a structured improvement objective. Second, conditioned on this objective, our remedy stage curates validated, stage-relevant experience and refines the policy via behavior-regularized offline reinforcement learning, without requiring costly online rollouts at each optimization step. Third, to safeguard existing skills, our retention stage constructs weight-space candidates between the inherited reference policy and the refined policy, evaluates them across the task suite, and promotes the best candidate as the reference state for the next generation.
  Evaluated across all 42 tasks of the RoboDojo-Sim benchmark, CSU-AI-07 ranks first on the leaderboard with a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 and Success Rate of 20.70%, outperforming the next-best entry by 5.92 points and 5.82 percentage points.

Robotics.title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
Robotics.summary: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
Robotics.comment: Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Modeling Uncertainty in Robotic World Models (UncertainWM). 20 pages, including 12 pages of supplementary material

Robotics.title: SCRUB: Contact-Based Surface-Frame Estimation for Force-Motion Control with an Armless Quadruped
Robotics.summary: Wiping, sanding, and inspection robots press a sliding tool on a surface with controlled force. Controlling that force needs the surface normal, which is unknown on real-world, unmapped surfaces. Surface-normal estimators can help estimate the surface normal, but they either need a friction model or assume that the instantaneous tool velocity lies along the surface; however, walking violates this assumption. We propose SCRUB, a contact-based surface-frame estimator, which lets an armless quadruped slide a body-mounted tool along near-vertical surfaces in the absence of known, axis-aligned, or vision-predicted normals. SCRUB's predictive controller presses and slides the tool using a Kalman-filter estimate of the normal from two cues: 1) A force cue measures the estimate's tilt across the motion. If friction directly opposes the motion, the cue is zero exactly when that tilt is zero, for any friction coefficient. However, if the cue's sliding direction is wrong, friction appears as a false tilt. 2) A velocity cue measures tilt along the motion. Walking and pressing move the tool in and out. SCRUB therefore subtracts the commanded press rate from the tool velocity, averages the result over each gait cycle, and treats this mean as lying along the surface. On Unitree Go1 hardware at nominal speed and load, SCRUB completed every wall traverse and column orbit. No orbit completed with either cue removed, without gait averaging, or with a fixed normal.

Robotics.title: Learning Soft Robotic Dynamics with Active Exploration
Robotics.summary: Soft robots offer adaptability and safety in unstructured environments, yet their compliant, high-dimensional, and nonlinear dynamics make modeling for control difficult. Existing data-driven approaches often fail to generalize, constrained by narrowly focused task demonstrations or inefficient random exploration. We introduce an uncertainty-aware active exploration framework that autonomously learns task-agnostic and generalizable dynamics models of soft robotic systems. We evaluate this framework on three simulated platforms---a continuum arm, an articulated fish in fluid, and a musculoskeletal leg---and on a real-world pneumatically actuated continuum arm. Compared with random exploration and task-specific baseline, our method achieves higher modeling accuracy by actively collecting informative data. This improved model quality yields higher returns in zero-shot control on unseen tasks and robust performance under sensing noise, actuation delays, and material nonlinearities. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-driven active exploration enables data-efficient dynamics learning across soft robotic morphologies, supporting autonomous and adaptable control for compliant robots.

Robotics.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
Robotics.summary: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

Robotics.title: Dynamic Shape Control of Soft Trunk Robots
Robotics.summary: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 hours on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.

Robotics.title: META-Robot: Self-Cognition and Capability Scaling in Agentic Robots
Robotics.summary: LLM-based robotic agent systems can generate programs for robot control, yet their generalization to new tasks often depends on elaborate scaffolding. Expanding their skill repertoires alone offers limited guidance on how to assess new capabilities or identify what remains beyond their reach. We introduce META-Robot, a framework that couples self cognition with capability scaling by expanding the criteria through which an agent evaluates and develops its skills. At its core, action-level predicates make execution outcomes explicit and available for LLM reasoning. The agent uses these assessments to identify its own limitations, extend relevant evaluation criteria, and guide the structured expansion of its skills. Proprioceptive feedback further grounds this process in the robot's physical state, enriching the evidence available for self-cognition. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate stronger overall task performance, generalization to new tasks, continued expansion of skills and evaluation criteria, and effective use of non-visual proprioceptive signals.

Robotics.title: FOSCo-Net: Ego-centric Voxel Completion for Forest LiDAR Occlusions
Robotics.summary: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.
Robotics.comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, accepted for presentation at ACIVS 2026 (23rd Advanced Concepts for Intelligent Vision Systems) Okinawa, Japan

Robotics.title: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
Robotics.summary: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.

Robotics.title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control
Robotics.summary: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.

Robotics.title: Learning to Live: A Step Toward Lifelong Embodied Intelligence
Robotics.summary: Embodied agents are usually organized around individual tasks, yet the physical world keeps changing between tasks and during execution. We introduce LIFE (Lifelong Intelligence from Experience), a framework in which a robot observes continuously, remembers selectively, and turns experience into new capabilities. RoboBeats, a family of lightweight streaming gates, tracks conditions set by the agent and discovers new events, deciding when an observation warrants a response or a memory write. Selected observations enter Plastic Memory, a flat store of images and structured records that keeps the source evidence, so new fields and indexes can be added when later questions need them. When existing tools fall short, Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM) turns solutions found during problem solving into validated, reusable tools and skills. Under matched protocols, RoboBeats substantially improves condition tracking over its base models and, at the same writing budget, retains more useful evidence for memory question answering than uniform sampling. A case study of limited scale, replaying 24 hours of continuous video recorded by a real robot, illustrates how the integrated system builds memory from a day of experience and uses it to answer everyday questions. LIFE takes a step toward robots that become more familiar with their surroundings and more capable through experience: learning not only to complete tasks, but to live in the world.

Robotics.title: Robocasa-Mem: Benchmarking Environment and Process Memory in Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
Robotics.summary: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.

Robotics.title: Multi-Agent Coordination via Support-Preserving Distillation
Robotics.summary: Offline MARL increasingly relies on generative policies to model multimodal joint behavior, typically by distilling a centralized teacher into decentralized one-step actors under the CTDE. We identify a failure mode at the teacher training stage: standard flow-based teachers pair noise with replay targets independently, so nearby noise samples can be routed toward conflicting coordination modes. The teacher then produces samples between valid modes, and because the distillation loss regresses each local actor onto the conditional mean of the teacher's output given local input, this error is not absorbed but propagated to the student. To remove this teacher-side artifact, we propose Mode-Support Semi-Discrete Optimal Transport (MoSDOT), which summarizes multimodal replay into a finite mode support with prescribed capacities and uses conditional semi-discrete optimal transport to assign each noise sample to a single mode before teacher training. We additionally study a shared-randomness variant that uses a shared noise component at execution to expose the residual gap intrinsic to strict-product execution. On controlled diagnostics and offline MARL benchmarks, MoSDOT improves endpoint quality and routing consistency, particularly on datasets exhibiting multimodal joint behavior.

Robotics.title: MARLIN: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Guided by Language-Based Inter-Robot Negotiation
Robotics.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning is a key method for training multi-robot systems. Through rewarding or punishing robots over a series of episodes according to their performance, they can be trained and then deployed in the real world. However, poorly trained policies can lead to unsafe behaviour during early training stages. We introduce Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning guided by language-based Inter-robot Negotiation (MARLIN), a hybrid framework in which large language models provide high-level planning before the reinforcement learning policy has learned effective behaviours. Robots use language models to negotiate actions and generate plans that guide policy learning. The system dynamically switches between reinforcement learning and language-model-based negotiation during training, enabling more effective exploration. MARLIN is evaluated using both simulated and physical robots with local and remote language models. Results show that, compared to standard multi-agent reinforcement learning, the hybrid approach achieves higher performance in early training with limited impact on the final performance. The code is available at https://github.com/SooratiLab/MARLIN.
Robotics.comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Accepted at ROBIO2026

Robotics.title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents
Robotics.summary: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.
Robotics.comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/speedym/failure-boundary-profiles. Data: https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/11195

Robotics.title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

Computational Geometry.title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
Computational Geometry.summary:
We provide sharp estimates on the number of vertices needed to approximate the Euclidean unit ball $B_d\subset\mathbb R^d$ with relative symmetric-difference volume error at most $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. We show that the minimum vertex budget $N_\varepsilon(d)$ satisfies $$\log N_\varepsilon(d)\asymp d\log\left(1+\frac1{\varepsilon\sqrt d}\right).$$ In particular, $\exp(O(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ vertices suffice for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and all sufficiently large $d$. We also prove that achieving a fixed error $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ requires at least $Ω\bigl((\tfrac{1+\varepsilon}{2\sqrt\varepsilon})^{d-1}\bigr)$ facets, an exponential number in $d$. We extend our vertex approximation result to Gaussian symmetric-difference error, and give a positive answer to the question of De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio about subexponential vertex complexity for approximating Euclidean balls.
  We also disprove a Macbeath-type extremality principle for unrestricted vertex approximation. Whereas the ball uniformly maximizes the inscribed approximation error among all convex bodies (Macbeath, 1951), we show that approximating the hypercube $[-1,1]^d$ to relative error $\varepsilon$, with $δ:=1-\varepsilon$, requires $N\ge\fracδ{2}\exp(Ω(δ^2d/\log^2(2/δ)))$ vertices whenever $d\ge16\log(2/δ)$. Thus, when $d$ is large, the cube is harder to approximate than the ball in this sense.
  Finally, we determine the sharp dimensional order of the classical Laguerre-Delone triangulation number, showing that $\mathrm{ldel}_{d-1}=Θ(d^{-1/2})$ as $d\to\infty$. This improves both the upper bound of Ludwig, Schütt, and Werner and the lower bound of Böröczky by a factor of order $\sqrt d$. By classical asymptotic approximation theorems (Ludwig, 1999), this improvement applies to every convex body in $\mathbb R^d$ with $C^2$ boundary and positive Gaussian curvature.
Computational Geometry.comment: 71 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. v2: exposition and references revised for a broader audience

Computational Geometry.title: Counterexamples to the Happy Edge Conjecture in Plane Spanning Trees
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study the problem of reconfiguring plane, straight-line spanning trees on point sets in the plane. A flip is a reconfiguration step in which one edge of a tree is replaced with another, yielding again a plane spanning tree. For a given point set $P$, the flip graph has a vertex for each plane spanning tree on $P$, and an edge between any two trees that differ by a single flip.
  The folklore happy edge conjecture suggests that any edge shared by both the initial and the target tree (a happy edge) is never flipped in a shortest flip sequence. This conjecture was computationally verified for up to 10 points in convex position.
  In this paper, we disprove this conjecture both on general point sets and on point sets in convex position by providing two counterexamples on $16$ and $30$ points, respectively. The counterexample for point sets in general position also holds for compatible flips, while the happy edge property holds for compatible flips in convex point sets as shown by Aichholzer, Dorfer, and Vogtenhuber [GD 2025].

Computational Geometry.title: A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every Norm
Computational Geometry.summary: We establish an $Ω(d)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio of convex body chasing in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with movement costs measured in any norm. Previously, the best known lower bound valid across all norms was $Ω(d^{1/6})$, established by Papazov (2023); stronger lower bounds were known for $\ell_p$ norms, where Bubeck, Klartag, Lee, Li, and Sellke (2019) had established a lower bound of $Ω(\max\{\sqrt{d}, d^{1-1/p}\})$. In particular, a linear lower bound was known only for the $\ell_\infty$ norm, realized by the standard construction of chasing faces of a hypercube. Our lower bound strictly improves on the prior universal and $\ell_p$ lower bounds for $p < \infty$ and shows that the functional Steiner point algorithm of Sellke (2023) - which has competitive ratio $O(d)$ - is asymptotically optimal for every norm. Our approach is based on the recursive construction of Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023) for metrical service systems, which gives a lower bound of $Ω(r^2)$ for requests of size $O(r)$. We show that requests in their construction, each comprising a set of discrete points in a graph metric, can be mapped to the vertices of convex requests in a $(2r+1)$-dimensional $\ell_p$ vector space while approximately preserving movement costs up to a factor of $O(r)$; the general result then follows via Milman's (1985) quotient-of-a-subspace theorem.
Computational Geometry.comment: Updates the previous version to extend the lower bound to all norms

Computational Geometry.title: A Two-Count Baseline for Change Detection on Dynamic Networks
Computational Geometry.summary: Change-point detectors for dynamic networks aim to find changes in how a network is connected. They are evaluated on real networks with labelled events, but many of these events also change how active the network is: how many vertices take part and how many edges are present. A detector can therefore score well by responding to activity alone, without detecting any change in structure. We test whether detectors from the literature beat a simple baseline that tracks only the number of active vertices and the number of edges in each snapshot, a baseline that we motivate with a standard statistical test for a change in activity. On ten datasets, four of them from the papers of published detectors, none of thirteen detectors ranks the labelled events significantly better than the baseline when the results are pooled (AUC $0.75$, or $0.73$ with scales taken from early snapshots only, against $0.66$ for the best detector). The baseline is best on only two datasets, however, and on the four datasets with the most events three detectors that track individual vertices score higher. When we rewire networks while keeping the degree of every vertex fixed, most detectors that ignore vertex identities barely respond, but several that track individual vertices do. New detectors should be compared with this baseline and tested at fixed degree.

Computational Geometry.title: Faster Planar Diameter using Pseudoline Envelopes
Computational Geometry.summary:
We give an improved algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ time algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter of Gawrychowski, Kaplan, Mozes, Sharir, and Weimann [SIAM J. Comput. 2021] and the recent $\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})$ time algorithm for unweighted undirected planar diameter of Fredslund-Hansen, Mozes, and Weimann [SOSA 2027].
  The main new result is an improved data structure for computing the farthest vertex when given feasible planar distances to the vertices on the outer face. The critical insight is the fact that normalized distances to the vertices of a face behave like pseudolines, for which we can leverage range searching and upper envelope data structures. Using the farthest vertex data structure, we are able to compute all vertex eccentricities and diameter in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$.

Computational Geometry.title: Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Pole-Aware Planar Preconditioning
Computational Geometry.summary: Surface parameterization is a fundamental task in geometry processing and shape analysis. For topologically closed surfaces, it is common to parameterize them onto a standardized closed domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with a prime example being a unit sphere for genus-0 closed surfaces. Many mapping methods use planar projections and perform computations on the plane rather than directly on the 3D surface. However, perturbations introduced before projection or geometric evolution propagate through the computation and may affect map quality, convergence, stopping behavior, and geometric validity. In this work, we formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input--output problem, separating smooth propagation through active Jacobians from changes in anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events. Under consistent piecewise-linear assembly, the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction in the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization reduces exactly to source-mesh harmonic extension. On a fixed-anchor branch, the corrected map factors into chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection, yielding an explicit sensitivity Jacobian and a finite-triangle conditioning bound. Separately, we introduce a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy and evaluate candidates on the corrected spherical map. Across 30 genus-0 surfaces, it reduces median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortion by $10.17\%$ and $10.97\%$, respectively, with both measures improving on every mesh. We also apply the framework to other spherical mapping methods including the conformalized mean-curvature flow and spherical density-equalizing maps. Altogether, our work highlights the importance of representation selection as a structural and practical component of spherical parameterization and downstream computation.

Computational Geometry.title: The Stretch Factor of Planar Delaunay Triangulations Is Nearly Determined
Computational Geometry.summary: The Delaunay triangulation is a classical geometric structure on a finite set of points in the plane. Its stretch factor is the largest ratio of the shortest-path distance along its edges to the Euclidean distance between the same two points. Determining the worst-case stretch factor of planar Delaunay triangulations is a long-standing open problem. We prove a uniform upper bound of 1.5949, improving the previous bound of 1.998 and narrowing the gap to the best known lower bound of 1.5932 from 0.4048 to less than 0.0017, nearly pinpointing the worst-case stretch factor. A central difficulty is that the line segment between two points may cross arbitrarily many triangles. Our progress accounting framework addresses this by converting the global bound into a family of local inequalities, each involving only a fixed number of real parameters regardless of the number of triangles crossed. Two further geometric lemmas make computer-assisted verification tractable: the pencil lemma decomposes each local transition into two geometrically independent stages, reducing verification over infinitely many possible next disks to a single differential condition; and the corner lemmas handle degenerate boundary cases where direct verification would fail. With these reductions, the proof ends with a finite verification of an explicit potential in exact rational arithmetic and outward-rounded interval arithmetic. Numerous geometric network constructions use the Delaunay stretch factor as a black box, so the tighter bound directly improves stretch-factor guarantees for a range of downstream applications, including bounded-degree plane spanners and low-weight spanners.
Computational Geometry.comment: 67 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables. Substantially revised: the upper bound is improved from 1.65 to 1.5949, and the title has changed. Verification data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23835635

Computational Geometry.title: A $(3+ε)$-Approximation for Fair $k$-Means and a Matching Lower Bound
Computational Geometry.summary: Fair clustering aims to prevent algorithmic bias against protected groups. We study Euclidean fair $k$-means, in which the proportion of each protected group in every cluster lies between prescribed lower and upper bounds. Because these constraints violate the nearest-center assignment property, center selection is coupled with point assignment. We introduce the drift-regularized relaxation, a new convex relaxation solved by a modified Frank-Wolfe method with linear-programming iterations, whose optimality condition controls the cost of converting its solution into $k$ fair clusters. Combined with any $ρ$-approximation algorithm for weighted $k$-means, the relaxation yields an exactly fair fractional solution of cost at most $2ρ+1+ε$ times the fractional optimum, improving the previous ratio $1+4ρ+ε$. In fixed dimension, this improves the best known ratio from $5+O(ε)$ to $3+O(ε)$. The fractional solution can be rounded to an integral one without changing the centers or increasing the cost, at a bounded additive violation of the fairness bounds. We also show that a $(3-δ)$-approximation is NP-hard for every fixed $δ>0$, even on the line with fractional assignments, so $3$ is the exact approximation threshold for fractional fair $k$-means in fixed dimension. The same guarantees hold for $k$-sparse Wasserstein barycenters, a special case of fractional fair $k$-means. More generally, they hold whenever every cluster must satisfy given homogeneous linear inequalities in the fractions of its points, such as a bound on the ratio between two groups or on the average of a numerical attribute in every cluster.

Computational Geometry.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Capacitated Clustering in Low Dimension with $(1+ε)k$ Centers
Computational Geometry.summary:
In many applications of $k$-median and $k$-means, including load balancing and redistricting, each center can serve only a bounded number of clients. This leads to capacitated clustering, in which a client may be forced to use a distant center because all nearby ones are full. This loss of locality defeats the techniques behind approximation schemes, and no constant-factor approximation is known in general metrics even for capacitated $k$-median. A long line of work therefore opens $K=k+\lfloorεk\rfloor$ centers for a fixed $ε\in(0,1]$, while respecting the capacities exactly.
  We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for uniform soft capacities in low dimension, that is, when the clients or the center locations have bounded doubling dimension. With $K$ centers, its ratio is $3-2ε$ for $k$-median and $9-8ε$ for $k$-means, or $5-4ε$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Apart from $k$-median in the plane, these are the first polynomial-time ratios bounded by a constant independent of $ε$; previously, the best ratio was $O(ε^{-2}\log(1/ε))$, even for $k$-median. We also obtain ratios that stay bounded as $ε\to0$ for non-uniform and hard capacities in low dimension, and ratios polylogarithmic in $1/ε$ in general metrics.
  Our approach starts from a simple structural observation: a near-optimal uncapacitated solution can be split into fewer than $2k$ capacity-respecting blocks, so $2k$ centers already suffice, one per block. Our main tool, the rescue lemma, shows that once every block that sends clients to a center of the optimal solution is rescued (given a private center), that center can be closed, so each extra center effectively rescues about two blocks. This lets $\lfloorεk\rfloor$ extra centers rescue nearly an $ε$-fraction of the blocks, yielding the linear dependence on $ε$ in our ratios.

Computational Geometry.title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness.
  Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.

Computational Geometry.title: Scalable Exact Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering via Sparse Geographic Distance Graphs
Computational Geometry.summary: Exact hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) of large spatial datasets is limited in practice by the $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time and memory required for the full pairwise distance matrix. We present GSHAC (Geographically Sparse Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering), a system that makes exact HAC feasible at scales of millions of geographic features on a commodity workstation. GSHAC replaces the distance matrix with a sparse geographic distance graph containing only pairs within a user-specified geodesic bound $h_{\max}$, constructed in $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot k)$ time via spatial indexing, where $k$ is the mean number of neighbors within $h_{\max}$. Connected components of this graph define independent subproblems, and we prove that the resulting assignments are exact for all standard linkage methods at any cut height $h \le h_{\max}$. For single linkage, an MST-based path keeps memory at $\mathcal{O}(n_k + m_k)$ per component. Applied to a global mining inventory ($n = 261{,}073$), the system completes in 12 s (109 MiB peak HAC memory) versus $\approx 545$ GiB for the dense baseline. On a 2-million-point GeoNames sample, all tested thresholds completed in under 3 minutes with peak memory under 3 GiB. We provide a scikit-learn-compatible implementation for direct integration into GIS workflows.

Computational Geometry.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for $(k,z)$-Clustering in Euclidean and Doubling Metrics
Computational Geometry.summary:
We determine the optimal worst-case size of strong coresets for $(k,z)$-clustering in Euclidean spaces and doubling metrics, up to polylogarithmic factors.
  In Euclidean space, previous lower bounds matched the best upper bounds only for $\varepsilon\gtrsim k^{-1/(z+2)}$. We close the gap for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$, establishing the optimal size $\widetildeΘ(\min\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\})$ for every fixed $z\ge1$, all $k\ge1$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Our lower bound replaces each offset in a previous hard instance by a group of distinct offsets. A fixed family of $k$-center queries and four-wise independent signs force a large relative cost error for every sufficiently small subset with arbitrary nonnegative weights.
  For doubling metrics of dimension $D$, we resolve the previously unmatched bounds for $z>2$. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde O(k^{2-2/z}D\varepsilon^{-2})$ and a lower bound that, together with known upper bounds, establishes the optimal size $\widetildeΘ(kD\min\{k^{1-2/z}\varepsilon^{-2},\,\varepsilon^{-z}\})$ for fixed $z>2$, $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_z$, and $D\ge C_z\log(2/\varepsilon)$, where $C_z>0$ and $\varepsilon_z\in(0,1)$ depend only on $z$. The lower bound exploits the ability to encode $Θ(D)$ independent signs per center without diluting relative cost discrepancy. For the upper bound, we use independent, unbiased two-point summaries that exactly preserve cluster mass and anchor cost, combined with iterative size reduction.

Computational Geometry.title: Strong Lower Bounds for Weak Epsilon-Nets
Computational Geometry.summary:
Let $P$ be a finite point set in $\mathbb{R}^d$. A weak $\varepsilon$-net for $P$ with respect to convex sets is a finite set $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ intersecting every convex set containing at least $\varepsilon|P|$ points of $P$. Determining their optimal worst-case size was described by Alon, Kalai, Matousek, and Meshulam [Adv. Appl. Math., 2002] as "one of the truly important open problems in combinatorial geometry."
  We give elementary constructions which establish the first polynomially superlinear lower bounds in fixed dimension. Already in $\mathbb{R}^3$, we construct point sets for which every weak $\varepsilon$-net has size $Ω(\varepsilon^{-3/2})$. More generally, for every fixed $d\ge3$, we obtain a lower bound of $Ω_d(\varepsilon^{-γ_d})$, where $γ_d=\sqrt{d/2}+O(1)$. Consequently, no upper bound of the form $O_d(\varepsilon^{-C})$ can hold with an absolute constant $C$ which is independent of the dimension. Despite the recent progress on upper bounds, the strongest previous general lower bound remained $Ω_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))$, due to Bukh, Matousek, and Nivasch [Israel J. Math., 2011]. To obtain our results, we apply a quadratic lift to grid-based configurations with many point-line incidences. The bounds also yield polynomial separations between fractional and integral piercing numbers of convex families, and lower bounds for Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers.

Computational Geometry.title: Constant Approximation of Fréchet Distance in Near-Linear Time
Computational Geometry.summary:
We give the first constant-factor approximation for the Fréchet distance in near-linear time. Given two polygonal curves in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $n$ and $m$ vertices, respectively, where $m\le n$, our deterministic algorithm runs in $O(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ time for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and $d$, with an approximation factor depending only on $\varepsilon$ and $d$. The same result holds for the discrete Fréchet distance. Our result extends the line of work initiated by Cheng, Huang, and Zhang (STOC 2025) from strongly subquadratic to near-linear time.
  Our algorithm recursively balances preprocessing and query time. An index for comparing subcurves of a single curve supports faster queries between different curves. We obtain this speedup by replacing one curve with surrogates assembled from indexed subcurves of the other and shared across starting points of matchings. Faster queries then reduce the cost of building the next index. Compact boundary reachability summaries allow the answers to be reused in later recursive calls. After a number of rounds depending only on $\varepsilon$, both preprocessing and query time are near-linear.

Computational Geometry.title: Quadratic Complexity of Voronoi Diagrams in $\mathbb{R}^3$ for Lines in a Single Ruling of a Regulus
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study nearest and farthest Voronoi diagrams of lines in three-dimensional Euclidean space, which partition space according to the closest and farthest input lines, respectively. For arbitrary lines, a gap remains between the known quadratic lower bound and near-cubic upper bounds for the complexity of the nearest diagram. We consider input lines chosen from one of two continuous families of straight lines on a smooth surface defined by a quadratic equation, with one line from each family passing through every point of the surface.
  Under the geometric assumptions stated in the paper, we prove quadratic upper bounds on the total number of vertices, edges, faces, and connected three-dimensional regions in both diagrams. We also construct quadratically many nearest vertices using lines from a single family on one fixed surface, establishing a tight quadratic worst-case bound. The farthest diagram has quadratic total complexity for every input satisfying our assumptions.
  Our proof uses a parametrization that arranges the input lines in a cyclic order and expresses tangency to a sphere by a polynomial equation of degree four. At a Voronoi vertex, the four tangent input lines give four distinct roots. The sign changes between these roots, together with the nearest or farthest condition, force two intervening parameter intervals to contain no other input parameters. Thus, only quadratically many choices of four lines can define a vertex, and each choice yields at most eight isolated candidate centers.
Computational Geometry.comment: Added a coauthor, more detailed explanations of algebraic geometry, and additional figures

Computational Geometry.title: Binary Huffman Coding with Unequal Letter Costs Is NP-Complete
Computational Geometry.summary:
Binary prefix coding assigns prefix-free binary words to symbols to minimize their frequency-weighted cost. Huffman solved the equal-letter-cost case in polynomial time in 1952 [Proc. IRE'52]. For unequal letter costs, Karp gave an integer-programming formulation in 1961 [IRE Trans. Inf. Theory'61]. Exact polynomial-time algorithms for fixed integer costs were given by Golin and Rote [IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory'98] and Bradford, Golin, Larmore, and Rytter [J. Algorithms'02]. For input-dependent costs, Golin, Mathieu, and Young gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme [SICOMP'12]. The exact complexity when letter costs are part of the input had remained unresolved.
  We resolve this $65$-year-old problem by proving that deciding whether there exists a binary prefix-free code of frequency-weighted cost at most a given threshold is NP-complete, even when the letter costs are consecutive positive integers $(M,M+1)$ supplied as part of the input. All frequencies, letter costs, and thresholds are encoded in binary. Consequently, finding an optimal code is NP-hard.
  Our proof uses two polynomial-time reductions, starting from Planar Independent Set. The intermediate problem prescribes the number of leaves at each depth of a full ordered binary tree and minimizes a signed linear score on their sorted right-edge counts. The first reduction represents an independent-set verification program by a tree growing level by level. A fixed-profile identity converts narrow coordinate restrictions into linear penalties that enforce the computation. The second reduction adds large dyadic terms to the symbol frequencies to force prescribed depths. These terms contribute a constant to the weighted number of ones, leaving smaller signed perturbations to reproduce the tree score.

Computational Geometry.title: Algorithms for the Shortest Vector Problem in $2$-dimensional Lattices, Revisited
Computational Geometry.summary: Efficiently solving the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) in two-dimensional lattices holds practical significance in cryptography and computational geometry. While simpler than its high-dimensional counterpart, two-dimensional SVP motivates scalable solutions for high-dimensional lattices and benefits applications like sequence cipher cryptanalysis involving large integers. In this work, we first propose a novel definition of reduced bases and develop an efficient adaptive lattice reduction algorithm \textbf{CrossEuc} that strategically applies the Euclidean algorithm across dimensions. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{HVec}, a vectorized generalization of the Half-GCD algorithm originally defined for integers, which can efficiently halve the bit-length of two vectors and may have independent interest. By iteratively invoking \textbf{HVec}, our optimized algorithm \textbf{HVecSBP} achieves a reduced basis in $O(\log n M(n) )$ time for arbitrary input bases with bit-length $n$, where $M(n)$ denotes the cost of multiplying two $n$-bit integers. Compared to existing algorithms, our design is applicable to general forms of input lattices, eliminating the cost of pre-converting input bases to Hermite Normal Form (HNF). The comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that for the input lattice bases in HNF, the optimized algorithm \textbf{HVecSBP} achieves at least a $13.5\times$ efficiency improvement compared to existing methods. For general-form input lattice bases, converting them to HNF before applying \textbf{HVecSBP} offers only marginal advantages in extreme cases where the two basis vectors are nearly degenerate. However, as the linear dependency between input basis vectors decreases, directly employing \textbf{HVecSBP} yields increasingly significant efficiency gains, outperforming hybrid approaches that rely on prior \textbf{HNF} conversion.

Computational Geometry.title: Polyominoes Folding into Four and Five Distinct Boxes
Computational Geometry.summary: We present new results on polyomino nets that fold into four or five distinct boxes. With the help of AI, we first found examples with areas 532 and 2128, respectively. We analyze these examples and reduce their areas to 178 and 358, respectively. We also generalize the construction of the five-box net and show that infinitely many polyomino nets fold into five distinct boxes.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Game-Theoretic Decision Framework for Optimal Selection of Coordination Detection Methods in Multi-UAV Fleet Operations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Detecting coordination among unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) fleets operating in shared airspace and identifying the route-lead aircraft whose navigation decisions govern fleet behavior presents a fundamental speed--accuracy trade-off: fast methods enable real-time traffic management but sacrifice detection fidelity, while accurate methods may exceed the time budget for actionable airspace deconfliction. This paper presents a game-theoretic decision framework that resolves this trade-off by formulating method selection as a two-player zero-sum game between a Monitor (selecting computational methods and parameters) and Nature (selecting the unknown traffic scenario). We construct an end-to-end pipeline from trajectory surveillance data through eight candidate detection algorithms, a Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis characterizing their stochastic performance, and finally a multi-objective optimization layer that identifies Pareto-optimal method portfolios. The minimax solution provides a robust mixed strategy with a probability distribution over methods that guarantees worst-case performance regardless of scenario uncertainty. Experimental evaluation across 200 randomized configurations spanning 5--50 aircraft demonstrates that the framework recommends distinct method portfolios depending on operational priority: Koopman Phase dominates balanced (70.6%) and speed-priority (79.7%) profiles, while CRQA emerges as primary (47.4%) when route-lead identification is prioritized. The framework achieves a guaranteed game value of 0.29--0.53 (normalized utility) across all tested preference profiles, providing the first principled, scenario-adaptive methodology for computational method selection in UTM fleet monitoring operations.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Neural networks and games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Iterated Elimination of Dominated Mixed Strategies
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This note compares two iterated dominance procedures, one based on eliminating mixed strategies and one based on eliminating pure strategies. It shows that, in compact and continuous games, the mixed-strategy procedure can trail the pure-strategy procedure by at most one round: If the pure-strategy procedure terminates at round $M$, the mixed-strategy procedure terminates at either $M$ or $M+1$, and this bound is tight. It also provides two characterizations of the mixed-strategy procedure that are round-for-round equivalent to it and that require checking for improvements only against opponents' pure strategies.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Coalitions, Stability, and Majority Jackpots: Frameworks for Unifying Majoritarian and Proportional Allocation in Multiwinner Elections
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Social choice literature on multiwinner elections tends to focus on characterizing two distinct tasks: majoritarian representation and proportional representation. However, many real world systems can be viewed as operating between these two extremes, such as majority jackpot systems used in several countries throughout history. Towards the goal of better understanding these systems from a social choice perspective, we introduce two frameworks that encompass existing desiderata for majoritarian and proportional settings: coalitions, which encompasses properties such as fixed majority and solid coalitions; and stability, which encompasses various generalizations of Condorcet's criterion for single-winner elections, such as Gehrlein stability and local stability, among others. We develop theory and tools that characterize the mathematical and computational aspects of both frameworks across a wide array of preference structures (such as the unrestricted domain over candidates and the restricted domain of party lists). Building on this foundation, we shed new light on majority jackpot electoral systems, which to date have received limited mathematical analysis in the social choice literature.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Bulow-Klemperer Theorem for Bundling and Improved Approximation Bounds for Simple Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study simple auctions for one additive bidder whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for the optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the optimal revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and $\mathrm{BSPA}_2$ for the grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders.
  For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{BSPA}_2 \le 2\,\mathrm{BREV}$. Thus, one additional bidder lets a reserve-free second-price auction for the grand bundle match the optimal revenue from one bidder, regardless of the number of items. This gives a Bulow-Klemperer theorem for bundling and resolves an open question of Beyhaghi, Cai, Feng, Li, and Weinberg (EC 2025) on whether constant competition suffices for bundling. The factor-$2$ bundling approximation is also tight.
  For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{π^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). For the lower bound, we construct an instance in which pricing three disjoint bundles earns more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). Together, these results narrow the tight approximation ratio to the range $[2.11, 2.645]$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: GTI-mSEMP Framework : A Proposed Framework to Simulate Malware Propagation with Inclusion of Attacker-Defender Strategy
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The rapid proliferation of automated, multi-vector malware threats poses a significant risk to heterogeneous, resource constrained cyber-physical networks. Conventional epidemiological models often treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric maneuvers between an attacker and a defender. To address the gap, this paper proposes a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi- Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework. This paper analyzed and compared the operational trajectories of Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node populations across three different operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge and Hardened Defense. Numerical simulation results capture the real-time transient dynamics of the network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The proposed mathematical and numerical framework provides a rigorous foundation that can be deployed in highly adversarial network environments to evaluate dynamic malware propagation and predict localized node population states.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning vs. Optimizing Bidders in Budgeted Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The study of repeated interactions between a learner and a utility-maximizing optimizer has yielded deep insights into the manipulability of learning algorithms. However, existing literature primarily focuses on independent, unlinked rounds, largely ignoring the ubiquitous practical reality of budget constraints. In this paper, we study this interaction in repeated second-price auctions in a Bayesian setting between a learning agent and a strategic agent, both subject to strict budget constraints, showing that such cross-round constraints fundamentally alter the strategic landscape.
  First, we generalize the classic Stackelberg equilibrium to the Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium. We prove that an optimizer's optimal strategy in a budgeted setting requires time-multiplexing; for a $k$-dimensional budget constraint, the optimal strategy strictly decomposes into up to $k+1$ distinct phases, with each phase employing a possibly unique mixed strategy (the case of $k=0$ recovers the classic Stackelberg equilibrium where the optimizer repeatedly uses a single mixed strategy). Second, we address the intriguing question of non-manipulability. We prove that when the learner employs a standard Proportional controller (the "P" of the PID-controller) to pace their bids, the optimizer's utility is upper bounded by their objective value in the Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium baseline. By bounding the dynamics of the PID controller via a novel analysis, our results establish that this widely used control-theoretic heuristic is actually strategically robust.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning vs. Optimizing Players in Budgeted Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study repeated general games over $T$ rounds between a utility-maximizing optimizer and a learning agent, where budget constraints couple the players' decisions across rounds. Without budgets, low swap regret simultaneously guarantees the learner sublinear regret and caps the optimizer at its Stackelberg value. Budgets break this picture: adversarial no-regret becomes impossible, so the natural goals are non-manipulability---no adaptive optimizer earns more than $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + o(T)$, where $\mathtt{BSE}$ is its Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium value---and low stochastic regret when the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy.
  We give an efficient, budget-feasible learning algorithm that achieves both goals in every budgeted game: any adaptive optimizer, budgeted or not, earns at most $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + O(\sqrt{T})$ in expectation, and if the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy on each of a constant number of intervals, the learner has $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret on each such interval. Our learner best responds to forecasts of the optimizer's play that are calibrated in two novel senses, since under budgets the calibration that prevents manipulation no longer yields low stochastic regret. Response calibration, which conditions on the learner's own mixed response by embedding its continuous mixing weight as a step function in $L^2([-1,1])$, prevents manipulation without discretizing responses; dual-weighted Lagrangian calibration ensures low regret. Although low calibration error requires randomized forecasts---distributions over a continuous space that need not have a succinct representation or be directly computable---we construct such forecasts in polynomial time by simulating online gradient ascent.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Pareto-optimal Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling with Predictions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study preemptive single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predictions, where a prediction of the order of the jobs (or of their sizes) is available, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. An algorithm is $c$-consistent if it is $c$-competitive when the prediction is correct, and $R$-robust if it is $R$-competitive whatever the prediction. Since the introduction of this problem as one of the first examples of learning-augmented algorithms, the best possible trade-off between consistency and robustness has remained open. We determine it exactly for deterministic algorithms. For every $R>2$, we give an $R$-robust algorithm whose consistency is \[ c(R)=R\Big(1-\Big(1-\frac{R+2}{R^2}\Big)^{\frac R{R+2}}\Big), \] and we prove that no deterministic $R$-robust algorithm, with either predicted order or predicted job sizes, has better consistency. In particular, consistency $1+\varepsilon$ is achievable with robustness $\varepsilon^{-1/2}+\frac16+O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$, whereas all previous algorithms required robustness $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$. Our algorithm is greedy: it follows the predicted order as fast as possible, subject to the invariant that the cost paid so far is at most $R$ times the optimum of the instance in which every unfinished job would end immediately. The matching lower bound rests on the observation that every robust deterministic algorithm must satisfy the same invariant along its run on correct predictions. Furthermore, we give a simple randomized algorithm, using predicted sizes, with consistency $1+\varepsilon$ and robustness $(3\varepsilon)^{-1/2}+O(1)$, strictly below the deterministic frontier. The question of determining the Pareto-optimal frontier among randomized algorithms remains open.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Power and Limits of Money Burning in Bilateral Trade
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the power of money burning in bilateral trade. In this problem, a seller owns an indivisible item, a buyer would like to acquire it, and each of these two traders has a private value for the item and the values are sampled from independent distributions. We ask whether the traders can benefit from a mechanism that burns money, that is, one that charges the buyer more than it pays the seller, so that neither trader enjoys the difference (money burnt is a loss for the traders). Is it possible that the traders will ever be better off if the trade mechanism can burn money?
  For Bayesian incentive-compatible mechanisms and for deterministic dominant-strategy incentive-compatible (DSIC) mechanisms, it is known that money burning is always a waste and can only hurt the traders. Maybe surprisingly, we show that once a DSIC mechanism can use randomization, money burning can significantly benefit the traders, and the gain of each of them can be arbitrarily large. In contrast, we show that the power of DSIC randomized mechanisms that burn money is still very limited in the sense that they cannot guarantee any constant fraction of the first-best gains-from-trade.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Almost-MMS allocations with small agent redundancy
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
For a fixed $ε\ge 0$, let $ρ_{ε, n}$ be the maximum value of $ρ_n$ such that, in every allocation instance with $m$ indivisible goods and $(1 + ε)n$ agents, there is a subset of $n$ agents with the following property. The allocation instance restricted to only this subset of $n$ agents has an allocation that gives each agent at least $ρ_n$-fraction of her $n$-maximin share (MMS).
  When $ε> 0$ we refer to $εn$ as the {\em agent redundancy}. The case $ε= 0$ is the standard setting without agent redundancy, and we use $ρ_{0,n}$ and $ρ_n$ interchangeably.
  For allocation instances with additive valuations, % agents, it is known that $\frac{7}{9} \le ρ_n < 1-Ω(\frac{1}{\log^2 n})$ for every $n \ge 2$ (with stronger lower bounds for small $n$). It is an open question whether $ρ_n$ tends to~1 as $n$ grows. We show that with agent redundancy, the answer to this question is positive. That is, for every $ε> 0$, $ρ_{ε, n}$ tends to~1 as $n$ grows. A straightforward corollary of this result is that for every $c > 0$, if the number of items satisfies $m \le (2 - c)n$, then the answer is positive also for $ρ_n$ (with no agent redundancy).
