The interface passes 12 live control checks. Spectral feedback reduces one target color difference from 19.756 to 1.211 ΔE_76^*; all five targets improve in a separate comparison. These measurements demonstrate the concept in one configuration. The resulting software and protocols remain available for subsequent investigations.

Multiagent Systems.title: Distributed Marginal Return: A Communication-Efficient Algorithm for Multi-Agent Weapon Target Assignment
Multiagent Systems.summary: The Weapon-Target Assignment (WTA) problem in distributed multi-agent systems is challenged by limited situational awareness and communication constraints. Existing distributed methods, such as auction-consensus algorithms, typically assume task-value independence, a simplification that fails to capture the coupled effects of multi-weapon assignments. This paper introduces the Distributed Marginal Return (DMR) algorithm, a novel decentralized approach that generalizes auction-consensus frameworks. DMR enables agents to compute bids based on marginal return and uses a consensus protocol to resolve conflicts, allowing multiple non-conflicting proposals to be accepted in parallel for cooperative optimization with minimal communication. A key theoretical contribution is our proof that the marginal returns of non-conflicting bids are additive, a property that ensures global consistency and validates our parallel acceptance mechanism. Extensive simulations demonstrate that DMR significantly outperforms baseline algorithms in both solution quality and communication efficiency, offering a scalable and robust solution for real-world distributed command and control applications.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Published in the IEEE Systems Journal

Multiagent Systems.title: ATC: Agent Trajectory Control for Role-Contract Enforcement in Black-Box Multi-Agent Systems
Multiagent Systems.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems assign different responsibilities to different agents: one plans, another retrieves evidence, another verifies, another executes. This division of labor is only meaningful if each agent stays within the functions it is authorized to perform. Over many turns, however, an agent can produce a locally reasonable message that exercises authority belonging to another role: a verifier that begins planning, a retriever that asserts unsupported conclusions, an executor that changes state no one approved. We formalize this as role drift, a turn-level breach of an agent's role contract. We introduce Agent Trajectory Control (ATC), which makes each role's authority explicit as a contract and enforces it at the point where a message would enter the shared conversation. ATC scores a proposed output for out-of-role deviation, leakage into the functions of other roles, impermissible speech acts, and logical contract breaches, then computes a leakage-regularized target that constrains regeneration; the revised message is re-checked before admission. Enforcement acts on the message rather than the generator, so ATC governs agents whose internal representations are unavailable. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous teams, ATC improves task performance and role consistency while lowering role-drift energy relative to strong baselines spanning prompting, memory, workflow control, and activation editing, with the largest gains under explicit role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)

Multiagent Systems.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
Multiagent Systems.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)

Multiagent Systems.title: Interpretable Early Termination of Web Navigation Agents via Closed Sequential Pattern Mining
Multiagent Systems.summary: Web navigation agents built on open-weight language models fail often and fail late, with most of the tokens spent after the trajectory has become unrecoverable. Recent work has shown that early termination is a viable cost-reduction strategy, but existing approaches produce opaque termination decisions that do not support diagnosis or human oversight. In this work we apply closed sequential pattern mining (BIDE+) to K-step prefixes of agent execution traces to produce a small, human-reviewable failure-signature library that organizes into a four-category failure taxonomy with associated repair recommendations. We use a multi-variant evaluation protocol that explicitly removes contamination artifacts (zero-step crashes and trivially separable single-step successes) so that reported detection accuracy reflects behavioral discrimination rather than trace-length distributions. We evaluate our methodology on 1,544 MiniWoB++ traces collected from three open-weight language models, achieving the best F1 at K=3 on the Exclude-errors configuration across eight methods (0.717), recovering 88% of test-set failures within three steps, and supporting an early-termination policy that saves 26.3% of tokens at 92% precision.
Multiagent Systems.comment: In online proceedings of AI Agents for Discovery in the Wild (AID-Wild) Workshop at ACM CAIS 2026

Multiagent Systems.title: Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network With Multimodal Feature Selection for Cancer Multiomics Integration
Multiagent Systems.summary: The increase in high-dimensional multiomics data demands advanced integration models to capture the complexity of human diseases. Graph-based deep learning integration models, despite their promise, struggle with small patient cohorts and high-dimensional features, often applying independent feature selection without modeling relationships among omics. Furthermore, conventional graph-based omics models focus on homogeneous graphs, lacking multiple types of nodes and edges to capture diverse structures. We introduce a Heterogeneous Graph ATtention network for omics integration (HeteroGATomics) to improve cancer diagnosis. HeteroGATomics performs multimodal feature selection through a multi-agent system, creating dedicated networks of feature and patient similarity for each omics modality. These networks are then combined into one heterogeneous graph for learning holistic omics-specific representations and integrating predictions across modalities. Experiments on three cancer multiomics datasets show that HeteroGATomics outperforms baseline methods across most evaluation metrics in cancer diagnosis. External validation on an independent breast cancer cohort further demonstrates its generalizability, where HeteroGATomics outperforms graph-based multiomics integration methods across evaluation metrics. Moreover, HeteroGATomics enhances interpretability by identifying important biomarkers contributing to the diagnosis outcomes.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 46 pages, 18 figures

Multimedia.title: Scalable Neural Video Representation Compression
Multimedia.summary: Scalable video coding (SVC) encodes a video into a layered bitstream of a base layer and one or more enhancement layers, enabling decoding at different bitrate/quality/resolution operating points for diverse devices and network conditions. SVC has been incorporated into major video coding standards and has recently attracted growing interest for both scene-agnostic and scene-adaptive neural video codecs. Among the latter, implicit neural representation (INR) based codecs overfit a compact neural network to an individual video, offering fast decoding and competitive coding efficiency. However, research on scalable INR-based compression remains in its infancy: existing methods introduce additional network layers, which couple the bitrate with the decoding complexity and cannot match strong scalable/non-scalable codecs. This paper proposes S-NVRC, a scalable INR-based video codec that jointly supports fine-grained bitrate and decoding complexity scalability from a single embedded bitstream. It adopts a coarse-to-fine prefix for feature grids and a nested prefix for network layers, which scale bitrate and decoding complexity, respectively. With a single encoding, S-NVRC spans a wide range of bitrate and decoding complexity and outperforms SHM-12.4 and the multi-layer VTM-20.0 by 43.7% and 5.6% in BD-rate on the UVG dataset.

Multimedia.title: VIPBench: A Human-Aligned Benchmark for Voice Identity Perception in the Age of Voice Cloning
Multimedia.summary: Speaker-recognition benchmarks test how accurately a model recovers the speaker label of a recording, treating voice identity as a property of the person who produced it. However, these benchmarks do not evaluate how humans perceive voice identity. Whether a listener hears two voices as the same person has consequences for intellectual property rights, cybersecurity, and everyday life. We introduce the Voice Identity Perception benchmark (VIPBench), which contains 124,876 same-or-different judgments from 1,290 listeners on 9,800 recording pairs from 100 public figures. The pairs include real recordings, voice clones generated by a text-to-speech system, and morphs between two speakers' voices. We also define four tasks that evaluate the alignment between speaker-representation models and human identity perception. The first two tasks measure how well a model's similarity score predicts the proportion of listeners who respond "same" and the majority response. The other two measure whether a model and listeners find the same speaker pairs similar, and whether a model's relationship to listener judgments holds equally for real and synthetic recordings. We evaluate eleven publicly available speech models. Listener judgments diverge from speaker labels most often for voice clones: in 41% of responses, listeners judged a clone and a real recording of the same speaker to be different people. No model reaches the noise ceiling; the best model explains 61% of the explainable variance. Models trained with speaker labels align with listeners better than self-supervised models do, yet a model with a 12% error rate on speaker labels aligns with listeners as well as models with error rates below 2%. VIPBench enables the evaluation of speaker models against human perception on real, cloned, and morphed speech, and our results motivate training speaker models directly on listener judgments.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets (poster). 30 pages, 12 figures, 22 tables. Dataset and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sendfuze/vipbench

Multimedia.title: Cassette-Editor: An Agent Harness for Editing Video the Way You Do
Multimedia.summary: Coding agents work in an environment built for them: a compiler or a test checks each change and points to the fault, and version control keeps every change in a project people can continue. Video editing agents lack one: an edit's correctness shows only in the costly rendered video, which does not point to the decision at fault, and existing systems offer either editing operations that cover only anticipated edits or a script whose output is a video the user cannot keep editing. We present Cassette-Editor, a complete agent harness for video editing that lets the agent edit the way a person does: knowing what the project allows, seeing what each change affects, and revising from there. The agent writes patches of typed changes to the editor's timeline document. A schema check and a rulebook shared with manual editing check each patch before it commits; a rejected patch leaves the project unchanged and returns each problem located with repair options, and an accepted one becomes a step of the history the user also edits. Reads map source analysis to the frames of the current edit. Because manual gestures are writes in the same language, folded by the same executor and rulebook, the agent can express every change a manual edit makes to the project. On 31 editing requests with the model held fixed, the complete harness passed 89% of trials against 47% for the same model with ten basic editing operations and without the rulebook, at less than half the agent time and cost per successful request; the loss fell on requests at rule boundaries, composite edits, and undo, not on finding content.
Multimedia.comment: 13 pages, 10 figures, 4 tables. v3: replaces the preliminary case study with a controlled evaluation on 31 editing requests with the model held fixed (harness comparison, component ablations, and a controlled repair study); revised text and figures. Preprint; evaluation to be extended in a future version

Multimedia.title: VISTA: Vision-Language Integrated Semantic Triage Architecture for Online Face Clustering in Long Videos
Multimedia.summary: Clustering faces by identity in long, continuous video streams is a challenging task that serves as a building block for human-centric video analysis. The majority of existing face clustering models are offline, i.e., they assume the entire data to be available altogether. In many practical scenarios, however, the entire data is either unavailable or poses computational challenges to be processed in its entirety. A handful of online methods that exist rely on geometric visual features and simple thresholding techniques, which fail when the faces exhibit significant appearance variations in long, unconstrained videos. To this end, we present VISTA, the first vision language framework for online face clustering in long videos. VISTA leverages semantic reasoning in a controlled, uncertainty aware fashion to maintain both high cluster purity and long range identity continuity. This makes it robust to the variations in illumination, pose, and costume changes that the faces and characters exhibit in long real world videos. Extensive experiments on the VPCD benchmark dataset (with 15 full episodes from The Big Bang Theory [2007-2019], Buffy the Vampire Slayer [1997-2003], and Sherlock [2010-2017]) demonstrate that VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance, consistently improving over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline (COFC) under identical detector, embeddings, and evaluation protocol. Code and supplementary material: https://github.com/SkyJiashu/VISTA.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26). 17 pages, including 8 pages of supplementary material

Multimedia.title: DGC-Net: Cross-Modal Dynamic Routing with Global-Guided Compensation in Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
Multimedia.summary: User-generated videos, including opinion vlogs and video reviews, provide a rich source of people's attitudes toward products, services, and social topics. Understanding the sentiment expressed by speakers is important for analyzing online opinions, as transcripts alone may not capture the attitude and intensity conveyed through vocal tone and facial expressions. Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) addresses this need by integrating textual, acoustic, and visual cues. However, these cues are often subtle, noisy, and inconsistent across modalities. Existing local affective cue modeling methods typically operate within individual modalities and overlook global contexts from other modalities. This may cause cross-modal affective cue inconsistency. Hierarchical global-local fusion methods integrate global semantics with fine-grained local affective cues. However, they commonly determine the relative contributions of the two representations implicitly, preventing the global-local contributions from adapting to the sample-dependent reliability of local cues and resulting in either insufficient use of informative local cues or excessive interference from unreliable ones. To address these issues, we propose DGC-Net, a Dynamic Gating and Global-Guided Compensation Network for MSA. DGC-Net mitigates cross-modal affective cue inconsistency through cross-modal contribution-aware dynamic expert routing. This mechanism uses auxiliary global contexts to guide local expert selection. Moreover, global-guided dynamic compensation fusion alleviates sample-dependent global-local contribution imbalance while preserving global semantic as the primary anchor and adaptively incorporating expert-refined local cues. Experiments on five multimodal benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of DGC-Net, and ablation studies verify the contribution of each proposed component.

Multimedia.title: SparseGraph-I2P: Consistency-Guided Hypothesis Selection for Efficient Image-to-Point-Cloud Registration
Multimedia.summary: Coarse-to-fine image-to-point-cloud (I2P) registration risks discarding correct but ambiguous patch pairs, while retaining more candidates repeats fine matching over overlapping patches. SparseGraph-I2P aims to improve registration recall by increasing the inlier ratio at the pose solver, using sensor or monocular depth. A Coarse Hypothesis Graph combines appearance with depth-derived first- and second-order compatibility to select a fixed budget of patch pairs. Sparse Fine Matching decodes each queried pixel once and skips pixel--point comparisons covered by an ancestor patch paired with the same point-cloud region. With sensor depth, depth-aware filtering ranks correspondences by SC2 spectral support for a single EPnP solve. With monocular depth, depth or inverse depth is calibrated from correspondence geometry before filtering. SparseGraph-I2P achieves the highest registration recall and lowest latency among the compared methods on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes with sensor depth. With predicted depth, it retains the highest recall on RGB-D Scenes V2 at an additional calibration cost. Code will be released.
Multimedia.comment: 20 pages

Multimedia.title: LLMCodec: Adapting Video Codecs for Efficient Weight Compression of Large Language Models
Multimedia.summary: The rapid development of large language models(LLMs) has led to remarkable advances in natural language processing. However, the increasing scale of these models introduces substantial challenges in terms of storage, transmission, and deployment. Though great efforts have been devoted to model compression and quantization, existing methods often rely on fine-tuning or calibration data, which exhibit limited generalization across different tensor types. In this paper, we argue that video codecs offer a promising solution for LLM compression, due to their inherent compatibility with matrix structured data, configurable compression strategies, and the availability of highly optimized, off-the-shelf implementations. Therefore, we present LLMCodec, a video codec-based LLM compression method that integrates affine quantization with the recent VVC/H.266 video codec. Beyond VVC, we further compare a range of video codecs and encoding profiles to evaluate their impact on compression performance. Experiments on different models demonstrate the robustness and generality of LLMCodec. Notably, on LLaMA-3-8B at 2-bit precision, LLMCodec reduces perplexity by over 1.5x and improves downstream task accuracy by 21% compared with the existing method.

Multimedia.title: VideoZeroBench: Probing the Limits of Video MLLMs with Spatio-Temporal Evidence Verification
Multimedia.summary: Video multimodal large language models achieve strong results on existing benchmarks, but answer accuracy alone does not establish whether they can locate the evidence needed to answer a question. We introduce VideoZeroBench, a challenging long-video benchmark with manually annotated question-answer pairs spanning 13 video domains. Questions target fine-grained cues, fleeting events, and evidence distributed across multiple segments. Temporal intervals and key-frame boxes are annotated where applicable. All questions undergo two rounds of cross-verification for answer validity and evidence quality. Our five-level diagnostic protocol compares answering with and without evidence hints, then combines answer correctness with independently evaluated temporal and spatial grounding. Across 19 evaluated models, the best standard QA accuracy is 24.8% (Level-3), achieved by Gemini-3.7-Flash. No model exceeds 1.8% when correct answers and accurate spatio-temporal localization are jointly required (Level-5). Analyses of atomic abilities, evidence spans, input modalities, and thinking-with-videos inference further characterize where the evaluated systems struggle. These findings motivate more precise evidence search and localization for long-video question answering. Our code and data are publicly released.

Multimedia.title: Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection with Embedding-Space Explanations
Multimedia.summary: AI-generated images have reached unprecedented realism, while instruction-driven AI editors re-synthesize images for local changes, leaving no splice boundary to localize. Most detectors are black boxes with unverifiable verdicts and generalize poorly because adapting a backbone on the detection distribution memorizes generator-specific fingerprints that quickly become obsolete. Specialist detectors built on pure-vision representations, particularly DINOv3, generalize well across generators, but explainable methods forgo this advantage: jointly training one multimodal model for classification and language generation subjects its visual representation to the language objective. We therefore require that explanation training cannot alter the verdict. We introduce FOX, which first builds and locks a specialist DINOv3 detector, then uses its representation to guide a lightweight VLM toward forensic explanation. A joint-embedding predictor maps locked visual evidence into a frozen text encoder's semantic space, producing guidance that the VLM verbalizes on demand. FOX achieves 97.4 mean AUC across 14 unseen generators, 69.8 BERTScore on XPlainVerse, and 56.1 on LOKI.
Multimedia.comment: WACV 2027

Computational Geometry.title: Quadratic Reconfiguration of Plane Spanning Paths on Two-Layer Point Sets
Computational Geometry.summary: Consider a crossing-free polygonal path with $n$ vertices and a flip operation that removes an edge and adds another one, without changing the vertex set and keeping the path crossing free. It is conjectured that any two such paths can be transformed into each other by a sequence of flips. Recently, Kleist et al. (2024) proved the conjecture for the special cases of vertices arranged in two convex layers. However, the number of flips in their proof may be exponential. In this paper, we show that $O(n^2)$ flips suffice. More precisely, for a two-layer point set $S=L_0\cup L_1$, where $L_0$ and $L_1$ denote the outer and inner layers, respectively, our method uses $O(|L_0|+|L_1|^2)$ flips.

Computational Geometry.title: Non-simple Arrangements of Lines and Pseudolines with Many Triangles
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study affine arrangements of an even number $n$ of lines and pseudolines with many triangles. For simple ones, Blanc's bound limits the number of triangular faces to $\lfloor n(n-5/2)/3\rfloor$. Adapting the Bartholdi-Blanc-Loisel doubling to the even case, we construct an infinite series of arrangements of $n=6\cdot2^t+2$ ($8,14,26,50,\ldots$) straight lines with two triple points and $(n(n-5/2)+1)/3$ triangles, one more than the simple bound allows.
  We obtain exhaustive enumerations of triangle-maximal pseudoline arrangements, simple or not, for even $n\le12$. For $n=6,8,10,12,14$ the maximum number of triangles, for both lines and pseudolines, is $7,15,25,38,54$; for $n=8,12,14$ every optimal arrangement has multiple points. All optimal arrangements for even $n\le12$ are realizable by straight lines, except two arrangements of 10 pseudolines, which are not stretchable. For the odd value $n=11$, no arrangement with $33$ triangles exists even with multiple points.
  We also obtain even arrangements by adding a line to odd ones. For $n\equiv2\pmod 6$ this again gives one triangle more than the simple bound, in pseudolines up to $n=44$ and in straight lines for $n=20$ and $n=32$. Doubling these pseudoline arrangements gives members of the series $18\cdot2^t+2$ and $30\cdot2^t+2$ with the same excess, up to $n=146$ and $n=242$, respectively; those with $n=38$ and $n=74$ are realizable by straight lines.
  These results lead us to conjecture that an arrangement of an even number $n$ of pseudolines has at most $\lfloor n(n-2)/3\rfloor-\lfloor n/6\rfloor$ triangles.
Computational Geometry.comment: 72 pages, 19 figures, 8 tables. Code, enumeration outputs and certificates: https://github.com/parpalak/nonsimple-arrangements

Computational Geometry.title: Pair-Relative Partial Equivariance for Rotation-Robust Keypoint Descriptor Matching
Computational Geometry.summary: Learned keypoint descriptors trained on upright imagery often fail under large in-plane rotation. Steerers address this by applying a single exact SO(2) representation to the descriptor space, but this global group constraint can be too rigid for keypoint descriptors, whose angular responses need not follow a single group representation. We propose pair-relative partial equivariance, which measures equivariance under the empirical distribution of relative rotations in image pairs, and PaSteer, a relaxed descriptor-steering framework that allows the steering map to leave the exact representation manifold while retaining the lightweight, backbone-free design of steering. PaSteer instantiates this relaxation with two variants: an identity-preserving residual steerer (PaSteer-soft) and a free-form Fourier steerer (PaSteer-free). We show that the per-angle optimal linear steerer for a fixed non-equivariant descriptor generally does not obey the group composition law, explaining why exact representations can be suboptimal in the frozen-descriptor regime. On Roto-360, MegaDepth-1500, AIMS, and IMC-PT, PaSteer consistently improves rotation-robust matching over an exact steerer on frozen DeDoDe descriptors, especially under large relative rotations, with minimal upright degradation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Pareto Inefficiency of EFX
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We consider the problem of allocating indivisible goods to agents with additive valuations, under two classic notions of fairness and efficiency: envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) and Pareto optimality. While some of the earliest work on EFX showed that Pareto optimal EFX allocations may not exist if agents can have zero value for some goods, it has remained open whether the same is true when all values are positive.
  We present a simple instance in which every good has positive value to every agent, but no Pareto optimal EFX allocation exists. We then generalize to a family of instances showing that Pareto optimal $α$-EFX allocations may not exist for any $α> 2/3$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: An explicit solution of the five-expert prediction PDE and the exact optimality set of COMB
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In this paper, we derive an explicit solution of the stationary prediction with expert advice PDE for five experts. The formula is given in three regions. In the first two regions, it is the four-expert solution plus a single integral with an elementary positive density. In the third region, it is a finite sum of hyperbolic products whose coefficients are determined by one scalar quadrature. Our formula establishes that the rank ordered adversary $(1,0,1,0,0)$ achieves the Hamiltonian maximum in the PDE everywhere in the ordered sector, while the COMB strategy $(1,0,1,0,1)$ is optimal only on a lower dimensional subset of the sector (where $x_1=x_2$ and $x_3=x_4$). The verification of the Hamiltonian inequalities is a tedious task, part of which is completed with a computer assisted proof. The verification reduces to 21 scalar inequalities, which we prove using 147 exact rational Bernstein polynomial certificates. The exact certificates and their independent arithmetic checks are included in a supplement to this paper, and a Lean 4 formalization machine-checks the verification and both main theorems, apart from the viscosity characterization.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Second-Best Gains from Trade in Matching Markets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study gains from trade (GFT) in two-sided matching markets with independent private types and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The second-best benchmark is the maximum expected GFT achievable by a Bayesian incentive-compatible, interim individually rational mechanism that is strongly budget balanced at every report profile. These constraints generally preclude attaining the first-best GFT and raise the question of how much efficiency must be lost. We prove that the second-best GFT is at least one half of the first-best GFT in every such matching market. This recovers and generalizes the recent $1/2$ guarantee for bilateral trade by Liu, Qin, Ren, and Wang to markets with multiple buyers and sellers and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. Together with their matching upper bound for bilateral trade, our result establishes a tight worst-case ratio of $1/2$ for this general class of matching markets. Our proof builds on the virtual-GFT framework of Brüstle, Cai, Wu, and Zhao to reduce the problem to a one-parameter Lagrangian. The main step is a geometric, edge-by-edge analysis based on first-best edge-selection regions, combined with a randomized contraction in rank space. The same analysis also determines the exact worst-case efficiency for every level of outside subsidy. In particular, even a small outside subsidy can significantly improve the worst-case guarantee.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 44 pages, 2 figures; Updated with the section on Subsidized Markets

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: On inverse aggregate network assignment games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: To design platforms for multi-operator mobility markets coordinating their operations or infrastructure to support them, models are needed to understand the behavior of these operators and travelers in a shared network. Assignment games can prove useful, but operationalizing them requires adopting a more generalized aggregate assignment game framework that allows for identification and estimation. We extend such a framework to aggregate network assignment games, proposing a path-based formulation and a PURC-based formulation along with solution algorithms. An inverse optimization model is proposed for the link-based formulation. It is solved by a quadratic program that separates into a buyer block, which retains the node potentials and imposes every observed zero-flow cell, and a seller block. This estimator, introduced in the literature for uncapacitated route choice, is extended here to a capacitated two-sided market, with rationing prices supported on observed binding links and operator supply scales estimated by group. Computational tests with a toy network demonstrate the economic value of these models. A large-scale Long Island Rail Road network example (897 nodes, 671 census tracts, 123 LIRR stations, 8,320 directed links) is calibrated to 2026 fares, timetabled seat supply and National Transit Database operating costs. With 10-50% of links sampled, the misspecified inverse model fits oracle link flows with R^2>=96%. Held-out link error falls from 29% to 19%, correlations with the true rationing prices rise from 49% to 75%, and social optimal gross surplus is recovered within 6%. Deadweight loss is overestimated by 10-17%. Ablation tests show that ignoring the inactive cells more than doubles the held-out error and, at 30-50% sampling, roughly halves the correlation of the pricing wedge, while ignoring the rationing prices degrades every metric.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: At What Cost? (In)efficiency in First-Price Procurement Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions. We measure efficiency by the Price of Anarchy (PoA): the ratio between the expected social cost in equilibrium and the minimum expected social cost resulting from a socially optimal allocation. We first show that the standard first-price procurement auction has no bounded PoA guarantee. We construct equilibria in which every bidder is indifferent between all bids in a common interval, so that bids can be arbitrarily large, and the PoA is unbounded. If costs lie in an interval $[\underline c,\bar c]$ but bids are not restricted, the PoA equals the trivial ratio $\bar c/\underline c$. We hence study ways to restore a finite guarantee, first by characterizing the PoA when bids lie in $[\underline c,\bar c]$, which leads to the tight bound $1 + \frac1{e^2}(\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}-1)$. Alternatively, we introduce the notion of a phantom bidder: the auctioneer accepts the lowest bid only if it does not exceed a phantom bid, drawn independently of the costs, and otherwise buys from an outside option at cost $\bar c$. We show that a simple fixed phantom bid, i.e., a deterministic cap, gives PoA $=\frac1e\sqrt {\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}+O(1)$. We further show that no phantom mechanism whose construction depends only on the cost interval, under a mild regularity condition, whatever distribution it uses and whatever it reveals about the phantom bid before bidding, can improve on the $\sqrt{\frac{\bar c}{\underline c}}$ dependence.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Money Burning Mechanism Design: From Welfare to Surplus
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study mechanism design for consumer-surplus maximization, where the objective is the total value generated minus the payments charged to agents. This objective captures settings in which incentives rely on costly actions, such as waiting or effort, whose costs are lost rather than transferred. We settle the welfare-approximation question of Hartline and Roughgarden [HR08] by determining the exact worst-case loss from money burning in general multidimensional environments.
  For $n$ agents with arbitrary nonnegative valuations over a finite outcome space, we give a universally truthful, ex-post individually rational mechanism with nonnegative payments whose expected consumer surplus is at least a $1/H_n$ fraction of optimal welfare for every valuation profile, where $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n 1/k$. The mechanism requires no knowledge of the agents' value distributions. Nevertheless, the factor $H_n$ is worst-case optimal, including its constant, even for a single-item auction with a known i.i.d.\ prior and Bayesian incentive compatibility. Thus, the optimal worst-case loss is exactly the same for arbitrary multidimensional preferences as for a single item: neither the number of goods nor the complexity of preferences increases this loss.
  We further give black-box reductions from welfare approximation to consumer-surplus maximization. On valuation domains closed under scaling, any truthful, ex-post individually rational $α$-approximation for welfare with nonnegative payments yields an $O(α\log n)$-approximation for surplus while preserving these incentive properties. For known finite-support product priors and exact interim-value access, a Bayesian reduction converts arbitrary allocation algorithms, even nontruthful ones, into Bayesian incentive-compatible, ex-post individually rational mechanisms with nonnegative payments and an $H_n+\varepsilon$ loss for every $\varepsilon>0$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Cold-Start Pricing of LLM Services under Two-Sided Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Online large language model (LLM) services face a pricing cold start: providers initially lack the historical data and user information needed for precise pricing, while users' willingness to pay evolves with repeated use. We formulate this challenge as a \emph{two-sided learning} problem between a provider and a user. The user learns from private usage experience, whereas the provider incurs a serving cost and dynamically adapts prices using only purchase decisions to maximize cumulative profit. The provider's central challenge is to learn to price against an evolving willingness to pay without observing the private experiences driving that evolution.
  We establish matching upper and lower bounds on the minimax regret over horizon $T$, identifying two cost-dependent regimes. When serving costs are sufficiently low, our Calibration-and-Tracking (CAT) algorithm achieves the optimal rate $Θ(T^{1/3})$. In the higher-cost regime, where the provider must learn whether continued service is profitable, Calibration-and-Tracking with Retirement (CAT-R) attains the optimal rate $Θ(\sqrt{T})$. This phase transition shows that serving costs affect not only profit margins but also the fundamental difficulty of learning to price LLM services. Simulations support the predicted regret scaling and show that our algorithms outperform standard online learning baselines in the evaluated settings.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Verification Allocation in Stylized LLM Agent Pipelines under Hidden Tool Degradation: A Discrete-Time Mean-Field Analysis
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study a stylized verification-allocation model for role-structured pipelines with binary inherited corruption and hidden tool degradation. Standard contraction arguments give serial and multi-role fixed points and a finite-population deviation bound under independence. When verification actions affect neither future errors nor observations, the belief-state choice is myopic. We characterize a two-action threshold under an explicit monotonicity condition and a restricted four-action interval and tail policy when generation rates are equal and only one check degrades. Synthetic experiments check these model-specific results and find counterexamples outside the restriction. This is conditional model analysis, not a general mean-field-game result or empirical evidence about deployed LLM systems.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Limits of Finite-Sample Dependence Measures under Data Processing Inequality
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study dependence measures between two discrete random variables. The measures vanish at independence and satisfy the data processing inequality (DPI): stochastic post-processing of one variable cannot increase dependence. We ask which such measures admit an exactly unbiased estimator from a fixed finite number of i.i.d. samples, a property equivalent to being polynomial in the joint probabilities.
  We distinguish fixed-alphabet DPI, which preserves the alphabet size of the variable being processed, from dimension-changing DPI. Under one-sided fixed-alphabet DPI, every measure with a continuously differentiable extension to a neighborhood of the closed probability simplex vanishes whenever one processed state has zero probability. If the processed alphabet is larger than the other alphabet, the measure is identically zero. If it has $n$ states and the other alphabet has at least $n$, every nonzero polynomial measure has degree at least $2n$ and requires at least $2n$ samples for unbiased estimation. Both bounds are attained by the Gram determinant. Under one-sided dimension-changing DPI, every family with the same boundary regularity is identically zero.
  These results yield sharp task bounds for multi-task peer prediction. For two agents with $n$ signals each, $2n$ tasks are necessary and sufficient for nontrivial expected payments that vanish for independent reports and cannot increase under memoryless stochastic garbling. Under these requirements, unequal signal-space sizes force the larger-alphabet agent's expected payment to vanish identically for any finite number of tasks.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic Coalition Formation Under Capacity Constraints: A Regime-Switching Value-Investing Game
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Edge computing service deployment requires the Network Operator (NO) and Service Providers (SPs) to coordinate investment and resource allocation under uncertain demand. This paper develops an audit-based service management framework for daily coalition formation with fixed capacity and service-level agreement (SLA) reservations. A two-stage coalitional game separates infrastructure investment from operational participation. Demand follows a Geometric Random Walk (GRW), and SPs apply an ordered admission and suspension rule using reported marginal contributions. With the NO held fixed, the operational coalition value is submodular; mandatory reservations can produce negative Shapley payoffs. We derive a separable benchmark, compute operational Shapley allocations, and give a sufficient condition for convergence to an individual equilibrium. A probabilistic audit mechanism provides a conditional daily truthfulness guarantee under verified settlement and enforceable penalties. For five service classes over three years, the reference run gains 12.4% over static grand-coalition membership and recovers 94.6% of the full-information optimum. Across 30 runs, the median gain is 13.3%. Sensitivity tests examine policy parameters, capacity and alternative demand models. The gain depends on capacity and update order; abundant capacity can make the admission rule underperform static membership.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Decoupling Corruption and Horizon in Robust Contextual Pricing
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study robust repeated contextual pricing, where valuations depend linearly on the features. At each round $t\in[T]$, a seller observes a context, posts a price, and receives only a possibly corrupted binary sale feedback. When the seller knows an upper bound $C$ on the number of corrupted rounds, we design an algorithm with regret $\mathcal O(Cd+d^2\log T)$, where $d$ is the context dimension. This is the first guarantee for robust contextual pricing that separates the dependence on the corruption budget $C$ from the horizon $T$, closing the problem left open by Gupta, Guruganesh, Paes Leme, and Schneider (2025). In this work, we go even further by developing a randomized algorithm that attains regret of order $\mathcal{O}(Cd+d^2\log T+d\log^2T)$ with high probability, without knowing the number of corrupted rounds $C$. Finally, we show that randomized algorithms that do not know $C$ cannot guarantee regret of order $\mathcal{O}(C)+o(\log^2 T)$ with high probability, even in the one dimensional non-contextual case.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Cooperative Game-Theoretic Framework for Real-Time Deviation Settlement in Local Energy Communities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This paper proposes a cooperative game-theoretical framework for the financial settlement of real-time deviations in Community-Based Local Energy Markets (CB-LEMs). The real-time settlement process is modeled as a transferable-utility cooperative game, and the resulting Real-Time Local Energy Market (RTLEM) game is shown to be superadditive and balanced. We analyze two game-theoretical allocation mechanisms, the Shapley value and the nucleolus, and evaluate their efficiency, individual rationality, coalitional rationality, and temporal-aggregation properties. We subsequently compare these mechanisms with a settlement rule based on proportional imbalance responsibility. The three mechanisms are efficient and individually rational, but only the nucleolus is guaranteed to satisfy coalitional rationality for every RTLEM instance. The proposed framework is demonstrated using real-world data from a residential energy community in Amsterdam, showing the trade-offs among the three allocation mechanisms in terms of surplus distribution, coalitional stability, interpretability, and computational requirements.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: DisC: Incentive Design for Green, Robust, and Fair Client Self-Participation in OTA Federated Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Over-the-Air Federated Learning (OTA-FL) improves communication efficiency by exploiting waveform superposition over wireless Multiple-Access Channels (MAC). However, client heterogeneity, fading, energy constraints, and participation imbalance can degrade both fairness and aggregation accuracy. Existing Pareto-oriented fair OTA-FL schemes may still suffer from large aggregation distortion when highly weighted clients experience poor channel conditions. This paper proposes DisC, a game-theoretic distributed client selection framework for fairness-aware, channel-aware, and energy-efficient OTA-FL. Each client selects its participation level by maximizing a utility that captures Pareto fairness importance, learning relevance, OTA distortion, energy consumption, and delay. We show that DisC admits a Nash equilibrium and can be formulated as an exact potential game, where stable equilibria correspond to locally optimal OTA-FL operating points. DisC therefore offers a distributed, incentive-compatible alternative to centralized client selection under wireless and resource constraints.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE GLOBECOM 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Entropy Bounds for Local Coordination and Graph Amenability
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study local coordination on finite graphs, equivalently, the ability of randomized local protocols with independent private randomness to produce highly correlated outputs at neighboring vertices. Hutchcroft, Rospuskova, and Tamuz (2026) showed that if such local coordination can be achieved with low cost, then the graph admits a low-cost leader profile, or equivalently an appropriate bounded-radius decomposition, with a square-root loss in the cost.
  We substantially improve this bound for unbiased binary outputs. If the average disagreement is $\varepsilon$, we construct a leader profile of cost $O(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))$. The key ingredient is an information-theoretic influence measure: after fixing an ordering of the independent information sources, we assign to each binary output the increments of mutual information revealed along that ordering. For two outputs that disagree with probability $p$, the corresponding measures are within binary entropy $h(p)$ in total variation. Combined with a grand coupling theorem, this yields the improved bound.
  We also show that a universal linear bound is impossible. We construct graphs with binary local profiles of cost $O(\varepsilon)$ for which every leader profile has cost $$ Ω\!\left(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\right). $$ The construction uses weighted majority functions and can be implemented as an action-symmetric Nash equilibrium, giving a negative answer to the question of HRT whether leader equilibria are always optimal up to a constant factor.
  Finally, we show that the binary assumption is essential: for general real-valued outputs, the square-root dependence of the HRT theorem is sharp up to a universal constant.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Persuasion by Parts
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Classical Bayesian persuasion assumes that an information designer can condition signals on the entire state. We propose persuasion by parts. In this model, the receiver's payoff from acting is $X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ for independent coordinates $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ observed by separate sources. The designer commits in advance to a product experiment, in which each source $i$ can condition its signal only on $X_i$. Given the signals, the receiver computes her posterior mean $y$ of $X$ and acts with probability $g(y)$, where $g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ is a nondecreasing function. The designer aims to maximize the probability of action.
  Let $V_{\mathrm{prod}}(g)$ and $V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)$ be the supremum probabilities of action under persuasion by parts and under joint persuasion, respectively. When the designer knows $g$, we show $$
  V_{\mathrm{prod}}(g) \;\ge\; c\,V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)^2 \qquad\text{for every nondecreasing } g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1], $$ where $c > 0$ is an absolute constant independent of $n$ and the prior; the exponent $2$ is tight. When $g$ is unknown, we construct a product experiment $Π$ from the prior alone, whose probability of action $V_Π(g)$ satisfies $$
  V_Π(g) \;\ge\; c_\varepsilon\,V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)^{2 + \varepsilon}
  \qquad\text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ and every nondecreasing } g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1], $$ where $c_\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\varepsilon$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) is a resource allocation scheme, addressing the problem of fair allocation of multiple resource types among users with heterogeneous demands for different types of resources. Based on Max-min Fairness, which is a well-established algorithm in the literature for allocating resources in single resource type scenarios, DRF generalises the main principle of maximising the minimum share given to any user to the multiple resource case. It has a number of desirable properties, such as Sharing Incentive, Envy-Freeness, Pareto Efficiency, and Strategy Proofness, that make it preferable over alternatives, and as such, it is widely adopted in distributed systems. In the present study, we revisit the original study and analyse the structure of the algorithm in closer view. The main contribution is an alternative algorithm, which approximates the DRF allocation in linear time, significantly improving over the original algorithm's pseudo-polynomial runtime. We name the new algorithm Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness (PDRF), after its main working principle. We provide bounds for approximating the original algorithm, and critically evaluate the agreements of aforementioned properties, comparing DRF and PDRF over them. It turns out that there is an adversarial strategy which forces DRF to unfairly allocate more resources to users who submit inflated demands. PDRF, on the other hand, favouring smaller demands, penalises such adversarial behaviour and creates incentive for users to submit their minimal demands.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: On the Convergence of Alternating Regret Matching Algorithms
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Alternating updates, that is, where each player is updated in turn, tend to typically perform better in regret matching algorithms than simultaneous updates. Alternation within the regret matching family has long been a central ingredient of practical solvers for zero-sum games. Yet our theoretical understanding is lagging behind. In this paper, we address this gap by developing a systematic way of analyzing such algorithms. Our framework centers on an alternating analog of the RVU property that we introduce, which we use to obtain the optimal $T^{-1}$ average-iterate convergence within this family. In particular, we establish this for two simple variants of predictive regret matching$^+$: i) increasing-regret predictive regret matching$^+$ and ii) half-prediction regret matching$^+$. Interestingly, we find that half prediction is the unique prediction multiplier that satisfies our alternating RVU property, giving it a strong theoretical justification.
  Going beyond average-iterate convergence, we refine our framework to obtain $T^{-1/2}$ best-iterate convergence and further establish convergence of their strategy profiles to a single Nash equilibrium, without assuming equilibrium uniqueness. We go on to establish separations between alternating and simultaneous updates, including a game in which half-prediction regret matching$^+$ converges under alternating updates but fails to converge in terms of the last iterate under simultaneous updates. This provides theoretical support for the empirical observation that alternation can stabilize learning dynamics. Finally, experiments on 15 game benchmarks demonstrate that the strong theoretical properties of the half-prediction mechanism translate to strong practical performance, being on par with state-of-the-art solvers.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Settling PROPm and PROPavg in Graphical Resource Allocation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study proportional fairness in graphical resource allocation, where agents are vertices, indivisible items are edges, and each item must be allocated to one of its two endpoints. It has been proved that PROP1 orientations always exist and PROPx orientations may not, but it has remained open whether the intermediate relaxations PROPm and PROPavg (both can be satisfied without graphical constraints) can always be satisfied. In this paper, we resolve this gap. We prove that PROPm orientations always exist for goods on multigraphs and can be computed efficiently. The guarantee extends to chores and a mixture of goods and chores. In sharp contrast, we show that PROPavg orientations need not exist, even for simple graphs with binary valuations, and that deciding their existence is NP-complete. We further quantify the efficiency loss of PROPm: for goods, the price of PROPm is exactly $2$, which is one of the few settings where a constant bound on the price of fairness can be obtained. We complement these results with hardness results for welfare optimization under PROPm and for the existence of orientations that are simultaneously PROPm and Pareto optimal.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Full version of a paper to appear in WINE 2026. V2 includes an extended related work section

Emerging Technologies.title: qLevelPlace: A Level-Based Placement Framework for RSFQ Circuits
Emerging Technologies.summary: Rapid Single Flux Quantum (RSFQ) logic can operate at ultra-high clock frequencies; however, its physical design is complicated by explicit splitter trees and deep gate-level pipelines in which every logic gate is clocked. To address this challenge, we present qLevelPlace, a level-based placement framework for RSFQ circuits. We separate gate and splitter placement into two stages to better support levelguided gate-to-row assignment and use a timing-aware quadratic cost function to penalize long interconnects. Experiments on the benchmark circuits show that, on average, qLevelPlace achieves a $2.65\times$ higher clock frequency and a 51% reduction in layout area compared with the state-of-the-art RSFQ placer qPlace.

Emerging Technologies.title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
Emerging Technologies.summary: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly advise backers on which crowdfunding campaigns to support. LLMs have known race and gender problems, and it is unsettled whether they reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. We ask when, and through which decision process, LLM assistants use founders' gender and ethnicity. In a pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomized quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas and a persona-free control (40,248 responses). By default, founder names barely matter: under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero. When the backer wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favor Black-signaled (+8.1 percentage points; positive in all seven models) and female-signaled (+5.1) founders. They do so most strongly among near-tied campaigns and for the founder who alone carries the signal, and they almost never name gender or ethnicity in their reasons. The results fit an agency account of algorithmic discrimination: an aligned assistant takes its demographic preferences from its user rather than from its training data.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; includes online appendix. Accepted manuscript of the article published in Journal of Business Venturing Insights 26 (2026) e00682. Data, design files and code: https://github.com/Mirza-Samad-Ahmed-Baig/Whose-startup-does-the-AI-back-

Emerging Technologies.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
Emerging Technologies.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.

Emerging Technologies.title: Classical State Preparation for Variational Quantum Algorithms via Reinforcement Learning
Emerging Technologies.summary: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) potentially offer a pathway to practical quantum advantage, but their optimization is heavily hindered by barren plateaus and numerous local minima. While classically simulable Clifford circuits can warm-start VQAs to accelerate convergence, existing heuristic-based initialization methods struggle to scale within vast combinatorial search spaces. We address this bottleneck with CRiSP (a Clifford Reinforcement Learning agent for State Preparation), which casts Clifford prefix selection as a sequential decision-making problem. CRiSP utilizes Neural-Guided Monte Carlo Tree Search, driven by a Transformer-based policy trained via self-play, to insert learned Clifford gates before fixed parameterized rotations. This enables the construction of high-quality initial states entirely through polynomial-time classical stabilizer simulation. By integrating a curriculum learning strategy that progressively expands the search horizon, the agent efficiently scales to deep circuits. Evaluated on QAOA benchmarks of up to $22$ qubits and $1{,}370$ parameters, CRiSP outperforms state-of-the-art Clifford initialization methods by a mean of $3.19\times$ (max $45.02\times$) in average energy accuracy and $2.41\times$ (max $16.01\times$) in best-achieved energy accuracy. Assessments on VQE tasks further demonstrate the framework's robustness and generalizability.

Emerging Technologies.title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform
Emerging Technologies.summary:
Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification.
  Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond.
  The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

Emerging Technologies.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for BD-RIS-Assisted Multi-UAV RSMA Communications
Emerging Technologies.summary: Beyond-diagonal reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (BD-RISs) extend conventional diagonal RISs by allowing controllable coupling among reflecting elements. This flexibility is attractive for aerial networks, where unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) face rapidly varying channels and strict power limits. In this paper, we study a hybrid BD-RIS-assisted multi-UAV rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) downlink, in which UAVs within favourable BD-RIS coverage use both direct and BD-RIS-aided links, whereas the remaining UAVs are served through direct links only. We formulate a network sum-rate maximization problem that jointly optimizes UAV trajectories, RSMA common-rate allocation, beamforming, BD-RIS scattering matrices, and UAV-BD-RIS association. The resulting mixed-integer non-convex problem is solved by using deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm, equipped with a constraint-preserving action layer that generates reciprocal and lossless BD-RIS responses in closed form and handles the binary association inside the environment transition. Simulation results, averaged over three training seeds under a physically consistent channel model with blocked direct links near the BD-RISs, show that the proposed design attains a sum rate comparable to SAC and higher than twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient ( TD3), proximal policy optimization (PPO), and deep Q-network (DQN), exceeds per-slot alternating optimization with fixed trajectories at about 1/65 of its per-slot runtime, and benefits mainly from RSMA, while the additional BD-RIS gain is modest.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, accepted for presentation at the IEEE GLOBECOM 2026 Workshops

Emerging Technologies.title: Defining Autonomous Weapon Systems: A schematic framework for refined purpose-driven definitions
Emerging Technologies.summary: The literature on autonomous weapon systems (AWS) includes many proposed definitions for these (types of) systems, with core disagreements between scholars, governments, and international regulatory bodies. In this article, we present and critique prevailing (classes of) definitions, arguing that what is needed is not a singular definition, but rather a definitional framework which allows one to classify different sorts of AWS within the same conceptual family. Recognizing we cannot foresee all future AWS, we show how variations on a broadly accepted definition can be used to produce a definitional schema which can be easily modified in order to classify various concepts belonging to the class of AWS.

Emerging Technologies.title: Molecular Communication for Plaque Sensing in a Vascular Bifurcation with Receiver Constraints
Emerging Technologies.summary: Future molecular communication (MC) networks are envisioned to use the human cardiovascular system as a channel. Disease-related changes affect particle transport, allowing an MC receiver to also act as a sensor. In this work, we investigate plaque formation in a carotid bifurcation through a systematic fluid-dynamics simulation study with non-Newtonian blood rheology. We analyze how plaque geometry changes branch-specific particle reception and timing, and use these observations to estimate plaque-induced channel obstruction. At an illustrative reference of only 128 emitted particles, a 250 ms observation window and 50 ms temporal resolution, a Ridge detector estimates maximum local channel-width reduction with a mean absolute error of 8.30 percentage points. We evaluate robustness across system constraints like particle budgets, observation windows, branch access, detection efficiency, count resolution, and synchronization. Coarse counting has little effect when timing features remain available, whereas limited temporal resolution and clock uncertainty substantially affect short-window estimates. Extending the observation window to 1 s reduces these timing-related penalties. The results establish a baseline for plaque sensing from constrained MC observations and identify receiver capabilities relevant to the Internet of Bio-Nano Things.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 6 pages, 8 figures; submitted to IEEE ICC for review; Alexander Wietfeld and Luiz C. P. Wille contributed equally to this work

Graphics.title: GPU-Native Real-Time Textured Mesh Reconstruction with Seam-Aware Multi-View Radiometric Correction
Graphics.summary: We present a GPU-native volumetric-video system for real-time reconstruction of graphics-compatible textured triangle meshes from multiple RGB-D sensors. Existing TSDF systems accelerate fusion and mesh extraction, but extending them to per-frame textured meshing adds CPU mesh processing, CPU-side texturing work, or extra CPU-GPU transfers between stages. After input staging, our method keeps the reconstruction and texturing stages (TSDF fusion, Marching Cubes, connected-component noise removal, view-based texture mapping, inpainting, and radiometric seam correction) resident on the GPU; no intermediate mesh or image data returns to the host between these stages. A fixed-size-array representation of mesh topology gives constant-time neighbor access on the GPU and makes the downstream mesh-level operations data-parallel. Because we texture each face from a single camera, exposure seams that vary smoothly across each image remain; we estimate a per-camera low-frequency gain field and bake it into the atlas on the GPU. On the CMU Panoptic dataset, our method is faster than the baselines at every tested voxel resolution and number of sensors, achieves peak speedups of more than an order of magnitude over CUDA-accelerated nvblox and CPU-based Open3D, and approaches an offline textured-meshing baseline in perceptual re-rendering quality.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 20 pages including appendix

Graphics.title: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time
Graphics.summary: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.
Graphics.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 23 pages (8 main + 3 references + 12 supplementary), 11 figures, 19 tables. Code: https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough

Graphics.title: PhysOmni: Physics-Grounded Multi-Object Scene Generation from a Single Image with Real-Time Interaction
Graphics.summary: Recent generative video models achieve impressive visual quality but remain constrained by limited physical consistency and controllability. Existing video generation methods provide minimal physical control, and single-image-to-3D conversion approaches often suffer from object interpenetration. Furthermore, physics-based scene-level 3D generation methods exhibit spatial misalignment, stylized artifacts, and inconsistencies with the input data, restricting their use in realistic interactive video synthesis. We propose PhysOmni, a training-free framework that converts a single image into a physically consistent and controllable video through holistic scene-level 3D reconstruction. By rep?resenting the full scene geometry in a unified spatial coordinate system, PhysOmni resolves object penetration and alignment ambiguity. Unlike prior methods, this formulation enables accurate scene?level multi-object interactions and introduces richer, complex control types for advanced mechanics?based manipulation. By decoupling simulation from rendering, PhysOmni bypasses latency-heavy priors, achieving real-time physical interaction previews paired while preserving photorealistic visual fidelity. Experimental results demonstrate that PhysOmni substantially outperforms prior methods in physical fidelity, spatial coherence, and controllability. Project Page: https://zephipage.github.io/PhysOmni/

Graphics.title: Parametric CAD Bench v3: Evaluating Agentic Parametric CAD Authoring from Text and Engineering Drawings
Graphics.summary: Producing an executable CAD script is not sufficient to establish that an agent has satisfied an engineering design request. Evaluation must also consider the resulting geometry, specified dimensions, and native CAD modeling history. We present Parametric CAD Bench v3, a 100-task benchmark comprising 30 text-to-CAD creation tasks, 30 text-to-CAD create-and-edit tasks, and 40 tasks that reconstruct mechanical parts from engineering drawings. Agents operate in a pinned FreeCAD environment and submit native CAD artifacts to a separate programmatic verifier. The primary metric is mean continuous task reward, combining geometry similarity and specification consistency rather than binary task success. A September 24, 2026 snapshot covers 13 model-agent systems; Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest overall point estimate, 61.03%, and an image-to-CAD mean reward of 84.66%. These measurements describe complete systems, not isolated model capabilities. We release versioned tasks, evaluation configurations, and inspectable result artifacts.
Graphics.comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables. Benchmark: https://cadbench.ai/ ; tasks and leaderboard: https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/gnucleus-ai/cad-bench/v3 ; scoring code: https://github.com/gNucleus-AI/freecad-validator

Graphics.title: UniCross3D: Unified Cross-View and Cross-Domain Diffusion for Consistent Single-Image 3D Generation
Graphics.summary: Reconstructing detailed geometry and realistic appearance from a single RGB image is essential yet fundamentally challenging due to inherent ambiguities such as occlusion, lighting variations, and texture-geometry entanglement. While recent diffusion-based generative models have significantly improved novel view synthesis, existing approaches suffer from two critical limitations: lack of cross-view geometric consistency and insufficient cross-domain semantic alignment. To address these issues, we introduce UniCross3D, a unified cross-view and cross-domain diffusion framework designed explicitly for consistent and physically coherent 3D generation. UniCross3D features two novel contributions: (1) a cross-view latent regularization that enforces cross-view geometric consistency across synthesized viewpoints by penalizing latent variance, and (2) a cross-domain mutual information objective grounded in the physics of image formation, explicitly aligning synthesized color and normal maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniCross3D achieves significantly improved view consistency and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art methods and yields higher-fidelity reconstructions, particularly under challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.

Graphics.title: Camera-Free Object Discovery and Interaction with GazeTags
Graphics.summary: We present GazeTags, a camera- and computer-vision-free approach for worn head-gaze object awareness. Our small electronic tags cost roughly \$2 each and can operate for more than a year on a coin cell battery. They work in concert with a user-worn device (smartglasses, hearables, etc.) that periodically emits a focused infrared signal aligned with the user's head direction. Only GazeTags within that narrow head-oriented beam wake and respond, providing their identity and optional payloads such as object state or live sensor readings. By avoiding cameras and computer vision pipelines, our approach is very energy efficient, able to operate continuously even in battery-constrained wearables, and sidesteps non-trivial privacy issues. We describe our hardware design, characterize our system performance and operating tradeoffs, and demonstrate how GazeTags can enable practical gaze-aware environments.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Towards Trustworthy Physical Intelligence: From Theory to Practice Across Life Cycle
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Physical intelligence refers to intelligence systems that understand, reason about and act in accordance with the physical world and its underlying laws, dynamics, and constraints. Unlike conventional AI systems, physical intelligence interacts continuously with uncertain physical environments, and its actions produce consequences that are physically irreversible. As existing trustworthy AI frameworks have been developed primarily for digital AI systems, they do not fully capture the distinctive challenges of Physical Intelligence, such as physical safety, cyber-physical security, and physical manufacturing process. To address this gap, our paper develop a foundation for understanding, operationalizing, and governing trustworthy physical intelligence. First, we characterize the fundamental capabilities of physical intelligence. Second, we investigate the role of physical laws and principles in AI and analyze the associated challenges of physical intelligence. Third, we provide a unified structure of the end-to-end physical intelligence life cycle across five core stages and introduce the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence Operationalization (T-PAIO) framework. Fourth, we formulate the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence (T-PAI) Principles as a theoretical framework that synthesizes key trustworthiness dimensions and establishes a conceptual foundation for the governance of physical intelligence systems.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order.
