This work advances scalable, human-aligned assessment of communication quality in the operating room and provides a foundation for improving surgical teaching practices.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 38 pages, 6 figures (1-3 in the body, D1, D2, E1 in the appendices) and 14 tables

Multimedia.title: MemoCare: An Interactive Multimodal Mobile System for Automated Cognitive Screening
Multimedia.summary: MemoCare is a React Native mobile system for automated multimodal cognitive screening in English and Vietnamese. It integrates speech, temporal and spatial orientation, touchscreen interaction, and visuoconstruction. Google Speech-to-Text transcripts are scored with deterministic, task-specific rules. GPS-grounded current and historical administrative names support location scoring, touch events verify actions, and lightweight convolutional neural networks evaluate drawings. A separate model provides visual interpretation. Software verification passed 151/151 predefined language, spatial-answer, and touch-scoring regression cases and 48/48 fixed-coordinate spatial tests across four countries. Transcript-based tests exclude speech recognition accuracy. On a locked 71-image test set, validation-selected ShuffleNetV2 x1.5 achieved 91.33% mean balanced accuracy and 78.87% exact three-criterion accuracy. Four clinician co-authors rated the workflow (pooled median 4/5 across eight criteria; item medians 3-4.5), highlighting improvements needed in speech handling, response acceptance, and result transparency. The workflow automatically produces item-level and total scores.
Multimedia.comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the demonstration track at MMM 2027

Multimedia.title: SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
Multimedia.summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose **SHield**, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson $r \geq 0.991$) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of $\leq 0.13$~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across $1{,}600$ wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and $30\%$ opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable.
Multimedia.comment: 35 pages, 9 figures, 21 tables, 2 algorithms

Computational Geometry.title: Hamiltonian Cycle Construction in Rectangular Grid Graphs with Three-Stacked Triangular Holes
Computational Geometry.summary: The Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete for general grid graphs, while several structured classes admit efficient construction algorithms. In this paper, we investigate Hamiltonian cycle construction in rectangular grid graphs containing a three-stacked right-triangular hole. We explore two complementary approaches based on the geometric structure of the hole and the parity properties of rectangular subgraphs. The first approach constructs a Hamiltonian path in the complementary reversed staircase region, extends it into an inner Hamiltonian cycle, and merges it with a cycle in the surrounding graph. The second approach partitions the graph into six rectangular subgraphs and constructs a global Hamiltonian cycle by merging local cycles along compatible boundaries. When odd-sized rectangular subgraphs prevent direct cycle construction, we develop parity-based repartitioning techniques that transform selected configurations into even-sized rectangles. We provide constructions for adjacent and nonadjacent odd-sized configurations and investigate reductions for cases involving multiple odd-sized regions. These results establish a constructive framework for Hamiltonian cycles in grid graphs with staircase-shaped holes and identify the remaining cases requiring further analysis.

Computational Geometry.title: Catenary Visibility: A Geometric Framework for Planning with Tethered Robots
Computational Geometry.summary: This paper introduces \emph{catenary visibility}, a new geometric visibility concept for a robotic system consisting of a ground robot tethered to an aerial drone. The tether is modeled as an extensible catenary curve with bounded length, providing sustained power and significantly extending operational range. We define a point on the ground plane as \emph{catenary-visible} from a target point in 3D if there exists a collision-free catenary connecting them, given a set of obstacles. This paper introduces a geometric framework for visibility-aware planning of a tethered marsupial system, addressing the computational challenge of determining the feasible deployment locus: the collection of points in the ground plane that are catenary-visible from a given target in 3D space. We begin by solving the 2D subproblem, where the obstacles, target, and the ground vehicle's line of motion are all constrained to a single vertical plane. Our algorithm for this case computes the complete set of feasible launch points along the motion line and simultaneously determines the range of viable cable lengths for each. We also consider the query problem of finding all collision-free length ranges for a given location of the ground robot. Building upon this planar solution, we then generalize the approach to three dimensions, deriving a 3D solution for a constrained class of obstacles.

Computational Geometry.title: One Shot, Twenty-One Balls: A Computer-Assisted Proof of a Single-Stroke Total Clearance in an Idealized Model of Snooker
Computational Geometry.summary: Snooker folklore holds that no single stroke can pocket all twenty-one object balls. We examine the claim in an explicit model: twenty-two equal disks on a rectangle with six pocket points, under constant rolling deceleration, frictionless collisions with normal restitution, and lossy specular cushions. We exhibit a configuration and a stroke, and prove in interval arithmetic that every stroke in an explicit box around it pockets all twenty-one object balls, so the set of successful strokes has positive measure. That set is a ribbon: every speed from 9.3213 to 12 m/s works, while the certified window of directions is 9.4813e-43 radians wide, a number explained by a first-order analysis of twenty near-grazing collisions. A second configuration, a near-frozen cluster, has a certified window 9.4e-4 radians wide, thirty-nine orders of magnitude wider; its certificate uses Taylor models of degree six. The strokes with a given list of events form a semialgebraic set, and the endpoints of the windows are algebraic numbers. For the regulation opening position we state the corresponding conjecture, and show that if it holds with a regular witness then a finite certified search establishes it.
Computational Geometry.comment: 20 pages, 1 figure. v2: the witness of v1 was found not to survive exact arithmetic and is replaced by a certified one; adds the width and the lower edge of the ribbon, a second configuration with a wide window, and the semialgebraic structure. Code, data and certificates: https://github.com/avnerkantor/one-shot-twenty-one-balls (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23816267)

Computational Geometry.title: The Rhythm of the Tiles: Narrow and Low Temperature Computation and Simulation in Synchronous Tile Self-Assembly
Computational Geometry.summary:
In this paper, we prove that the synchronicity provided by the syncTAM can be leveraged to perform two additional feats impossible in the asynchronous aTAM. The aTAM has long been known to be equivalent to finite automata in the one-dimensional case. For our first set of results, we prove that this still holds when a finite, fixed amount of space is available in the second dimension. Yet, surprisingly, in the synchronous setting, a small, fixed, width is enough to simulate a Turing Machine. This holds even in the non-cooperative setting.
  For our second set of main results we prove that there exists a single set of syncTAM tiles that can be used to simulate any syncTAM system simply by using those tiles to create a scaled version of the seed structure of the original system and then letting the tiles from that set self-assemble from the scaled seed structure. While it has been shown (FOCS 2012) that such a tile set also exists in the aTAM for simulating all aTAM systems, that "intrinsically universal" (IU) tile set requires cooperativity (and is impossible without cooperativity as shown in SODA 2014). We prove there exists an IU tile set in the syncTAM that works without cooperativity. Furthermore, there exists a tile set that is IU for the class of directed systems (i.e. systems which each have a single terminal assembly) while remaining directed during simulation. This was shown to be impossible in the aTAM (FOCS 2016).
Computational Geometry.comment: 112 pages, 52 figures, Submission to the 2027 ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA27)

Computational Geometry.title: A General Theoretical Framework for Transformed Geometric Pattern Matching in Music
Computational Geometry.summary: In this paper, we present a framework of concepts, terminology and notation for geometric pattern matching, centred around the idea of a {\em transformation class}. After formally defining the concept of a transformation class, we provide detailed definitions of a number of specific transformation classes that are particularly relevant to pattern matching and pattern discovery in music, which is the primary application domain within which the framework has been developed. We then provide formal definitions of the notions of {\em match}, {\em occurrence}, {\em maximal match\/} and {\em maximal occurrence\/} and prove some results relating to these concepts. We then define and explore in detail the idea of an {\em occurrence set\/} and the more general notion of a {\em heterogeneous occurrence set}. Finally, we explore in detail the concept of {\em transformational equivalence}, including a consideration of {\em transformation groups}, along with the group-theoretic and transformational equivalence properties of selected transformation classes.
Computational Geometry.comment: 61 pages; 23 figures; draft of second chapter of forthcoming book

Computational Geometry.title: Implicit Additively Weighted Geodesic Voronoi Diagrams and Applications
Computational Geometry.summary:
Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $m$ vertices. After $O(m)$-time preprocessing of $P$, for any set $S$ of $n$ additively weighted point sites, we compute an implicit additively weighted geodesic Voronoi diagram in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time, supporting nearest-neighbor queries in $O(\log(n+m))$ time. In contrast, explicitly constructing the diagram requires $Ω(m)$ time. Our algorithm introduces a new sweep-line paradigm that avoids explicitly constructing the diagram, together with a novel technique for point location in implicit subdivisions.
  As applications, we obtain new dynamic data structures for additively weighted geodesic nearest-neighbor searching and the first efficient algorithms for shortest paths in geodesic disk graphs. After the same $O(m)$-time preprocessing, single-source shortest paths in a geodesic disk graph of $n$ sites can be computed in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time in the unweighted case and $O(n^{3/2}(\log n+\log^2 m))$ time in the weighted case. We also extend our techniques to implicit farthest geodesic Voronoi diagrams for unweighted sites, obtaining analogous bounds and dynamic farthest-neighbor data structures.

Computational Geometry.title: Optimal Average Distortion for Non-Expansive Embeddings of Euclidean Metrics into the Line: With applications to cut-matching games and vertex expansion
Computational Geometry.summary:
We show that any $n$-point Euclidean metric admits a non-expansive embedding into the line with average distortion at most $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}}\right)$, matching a known lower bound.
  We also present two applications of this result. First, we give a cut-player strategy with an optimal spectral guarantee for the undirected cut-matching game. Second, we give an improved spectral approximation for vertex expansion in high-degree graphs.

Computational Geometry.title: On the Column Number of Delta-Modular Matrices: an $O(m^2 Δ)$ Bound via the Shifted Heller Constant
Computational Geometry.summary: In this paper, we build on the analysis initiated by Averkov and Schymura (2022) and prove that the shifted Heller constant for matrices with $m$ rows is at most $m^2 + m$ for all sufficiently large $m$. Consequently, the number of distinct columns of a $Δ$-modular matrix $A \in Z^{m \times n}$ of rank $m$ is at most $O(m^2 Δ)$. This improves upon the earlier bounds of $O(m^4 Δ)$ and $O(m^2 Δ^2)$.

Computational Geometry.title: NumPSLA -- An experimental research tool for pseudoline arrangements and order types
Computational Geometry.summary: We present a program for enumerating all pseudoline arrangements with a small number of pseudolines and abstract order types of small point sets. This program supports computer experiments with these structures, and it complements the order-type database of Aichholzer, Aurenhammer, and Krasser. This system makes it practical to explore the abstract order types for 12 points, and the pseudoline arrangements of 11 pseudolines.
Computational Geometry.comment: 27 pages, 16 figures. Full version of a paper that has appeared (without appendices) in the 41st European Workshop on Computational Geometry, Liblice, Czech republic, April 9-11, 2025. Version 2: The entries in the lowest three lines of Table 6 have been corrected

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Fair Division of Chores with Upgrade Recourse
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the online fair division of indivisible chores among $n$ agents under upgrade recourse, where earlier assignments may be revised but each chore previously assigned to an agent must be replaced by a distinct chore that she finds no more costly. We show that a simple adaptation of round robin maintains envy-freeness up to one chore (EF1) together with a $(2-1/n)$-approximation of the maximin share (MMS), and that no deterministic algorithm without predictions can do better, even when all agents rank the chores in the same order. This stands in contrast to the allocation of goods, where the optimal MMS factor vanishes as $n$ grows and cannot be achieved together with EF1. Moreover, knowing only the number of chores modulo a period of length $O(n)$ (and nothing about the costs) suffices to improve upon this factor at the final configuration, while the same algorithm retains a factor below $3$ even if this information is wrong. On the other hand, envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX) essentially requires the exact number of chores: uncertainty between two consecutive values already rules out every finite approximation, and even exact knowledge does not allow EFX to be combined with an MMS guarantee better than the trivial factor of $n$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Transactions differ in how their value changes with execution time and relative position. Ethereum's EIP-1559 lets them compete through fee fields, but a fee bid gives no enforceable claim to an earlier position in the block, and no way to express willingness to accept a later one. Its base fee is a hard admission floor. We introduce temporal liquidity markets (TLM), a framework for crossing complementary temporal requirements: transactions seeking early-region execution (consumers) can fund transactions that opt into exclusion from that region (providers). Selected consumers complete within the early region and are ordered among themselves by authorization density, both validator-checked. In our block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers may be admitted below the base-fee floor. Under TLM regulation, funding-conditioned and capacity-capped provider gas is excluded from the ordinary EIP-1559 controller input. Counting it there instead raises the base fee and displaces ordinary demand at a positive base-fee fixed point. Exclusion lets the controller regulate ordinary demand at its original target and preserves the no-TLM ordinary allocation by construction; in synthetic experiments it raises total utilization with funded gas. Selected consumers pay their signed authorizations, which fund provider shortfalls; the surplus is burned. We state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties under it, among them validator-checked rule validity, full burn of the base fee, and no subsidy. An inserted consumer bid cannot raise any other consumer's charge. With a provider fee-cap floor, a small, capped inclusion fee and a consumer allowance tied to funded provider gas by a large enough link ratio, no finite set of consumer bids or providers that the builder inserts raises its direct fee payoff.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Motivated by a broad literature in psychology, organizational behavior, and matching markets, we introduce strategic tanking: an agent deliberately makes themselves less attractive to selected potential partners in order to improve their eventual assignment. Unlike traditional manipulation in stable matching, a tanker does not misreport whom they prefer; instead, they influence how others rank them. We show that tanking has a striking connection to classical preference manipulation. Cutoff tanking, in which an agent tanks with every potential partner below a chosen threshold, has exactly the same effect on the stable set as truncating one's own preference list at that threshold. Thus an agent can reproduce the power of a classical truncation while leaving their own preferences unchanged and every match acceptable. Arbitrary tanking, however, can go substantially further: under proposer-deferred acceptance, tanking equilibria can lie outside the sincere stable set. More broadly, whenever the sincere stable set contains multiple matchings, profitable strategic behavior remains available through either traditional preference manipulation or tanking, even when one side is restricted to honestly reporting their own preferences.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: From Scalar Games to Unconstrained Network Zero-Sum Games: Transfer Principles for Gradient-Based Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We show that, for a broad class of gradient-based learning rules, scalar zero-sum games form a complete test family for convergence in unconstrained network zero-sum games. Specifically, suppose a learning rule achieves last-iterate or time-average convergence on every scalar game of magnitude $a$ whenever $η\leq f(a)$, where $f$ is nonincreasing. Then the same guarantee holds on an arbitrary network zero-sum game with stacked game operator $\mathbf{G}$ whenever $η\leq f(\lVert\mathbf{G}\rVert_2)$. More generally, finite-time rate guarantees transfer mode by mode: the network response is bounded by the largest response of its scalar canonical games, and under compatible linear initialization conventions the worst-case finite-time network response is exactly the largest scalar canonical rate. Thus, understanding the learning dynamics on scalar games is sufficient to characterize universal convergence and worst-case rates over the corresponding class of network games. The result follows from the classical planar decomposition of real skew-symmetric game operators. Related mode-wise reasoning has appeared implicitly in spectral analyses of particular learning algorithms and in prior work using these decompositions for game representation and visualization; here we isolate the resulting transfer principle for gradient-based learning. We discuss implications for simplifying convergence analysis, time-average guarantees, low-dimensional geometric arguments, accelerated-method design, and worst-case numerical testing.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Index and Robustness of Mixed Equilibria: An Algebraic Approach
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We present two results regarding the relation of the index of equilibria and the index of fixed points, and the index of equilibria and payoff-robustness: any integer can be the index of an isolated completely mixed equilibrium of a finite game. In a particular class of isolated completely mixed equilibria, called monogenic, the index can be 0, +1 or -1 only. In this class non-zero index is equivalent to payoff-robustness. We also discuss extensions of the method of computation to extensive-form games, and cases where the equilibria might be located on the boundary of the strategy set. These results follow from a new method of computing indices of equilibria, which we also develop in this paper, that is based on algebraic properties of the system of polynomials describing completely mixed equilibria.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Kidney Exchange with Dual Donors
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Kidney exchange programs enable patients with incompatible living donors to receive transplants by exchanging donors with other patient-donor pairs. Existing models typically assume either that each patient enrolls with a single donor, or that at most one of a patient's multiple alternative donors is selected to donate. In practice, however, a patient may have access to multiple willing but incompatible donors who are all prepared to donate simultaneously if doing so enables the patient to receive a kidney.
  We study a dual-donor kidney exchange model, in which a patient may enroll with up to two proxy donors and the exchange is allowed to utilize both, provided the patient receives a compatible transplant. This paradigm allows a patient to participate in an exchange cycle via one donor while their second donor initiates a donation chain---unlocking additional transplants without relying on altruistic donors. We formulate the resulting combinatorial optimization problems under realistic cycle and chain constraints, showing that utilizing both donors introduces sharp computational challenges compared to standard exchange, and we design new approximation algorithms with provable guarantees. We also study strategic manipulation when patients hide a donor, establishing the limits of deterministic mechanisms and showing how randomization achieves truthfulness with near-optimal welfare. Finally, our experiments on realistic synthetic graphs demonstrate that using both donors yields substantial gains in total transplants over selecting at most one---even when only a small fraction of patients enroll with two donors.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Branch-and-Cut for Mixed-Integer Nash Equilibrium Problems
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We consider mixed-integer Nash equilibrium problems in which each player solves a mixed-integer optimization problem parameterized in the rivals' strategies. We distinguish standard Nash equilibrium problems (NEPs), where the parameterization acts only on the cost functions, and generalized NEPs (GNEPs), where the strategy spaces may also depend on the rivals' strategies. We introduce a branch-and-cut (B&C) algorithm for such games that, upon termination, either computes a pure Nash equilibrium or decides that none exists. The main idea is a bilevel reformulation based on the Nikaido--Isoda function. Using bilevel-optimization techniques, we obtain a tractable relaxation of this reformulation and embed it into a B&C framework. Depending on the setting, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of suitable cuts and finite termination. For GNEPs, we adapt intersection cuts (ICs) from bilevel and mixed-integer linear optimization. Such cuts exist under assumptions that hold, e.g., for pure-integer GNEPs with decoupled concave objectives and linear coupling constraints. Since ICs may become arbitrarily shallow, we complement them with a fallback strategy that fixes recurring integer profiles and ensures finite termination in a relevant setting. For NEPs, suitable cuts always exist via best-response inequalities, and our method terminates finitely whenever the set of best-response sets is finite. This holds, e.g., if (i) the cost functions are concave in the players' own continuous strategies and the strategy sets are polyhedral, or (ii) the cost functions only depend on the player's own strategy and the rivals' integer strategy components. Numerical results on various NEPs and GNEPs show that our tailored B&C method outperforms directly applying the state-of-the-art bilevel solver MibS on the tested integer and generalized knapsack instances.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, we establish for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial, and this remains true even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we extend the Dantzig counterpart in~\cite{zhongye2026} to the two-player setting and prove that it terminates at an optimal strategy profile. However, a similar counterexample construction establishes an exponential iteration lower bound for termination with unrestricted costs. This construction does not extend to unit weights, for which we prove that the algorithm admits a strongly polynomial implementation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Truthful and Admissible Principal--Agent Testing with Nuisance Parameters
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Accelerating Min-Max Optimization via Power-Law Stepsizes
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We revisit the convergence guarantees of the Extragradient (EG) method for unconstrained biaffine min-max optimization. It is known that EG with a fixed stepsize achieves a $Θ(T^{-1/2})$ last-iterate convergence rate, which is slower than the optimal $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ rate attainable by incorporating additional mechanisms such as anchoring. Motivated by recent advances showing that dynamic stepsizes alone can significantly accelerate gradient descent, we ask whether dynamic stepsizes can similarly accelerate the last-iterate convergence of EG.
  We present the first positive result in this direction. Specifically, we provide a deterministic dynamic stepsize schedule that accelerates the convergence rate of EG to $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2/3+\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$. We also show that this rate is nearly tight when the extrapolation and update steps of EG use the same stepsize. We then show that allowing different stepsizes for the extrapolation and update steps further improves the convergence rate to the near-optimal $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1+\varepsilon})$. Our analysis reduces stepsize scheduling to an optimization problem, whose solution leads to a stepsize schedule that follows (a discretization of) a power-law distribution. Our proposed stepsize schedules and analysis extend to other methods, such as Optimistic Gradient (OG), and suggest broader applicability to general min-max optimization problems.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Competitive Ratio of Online Budgeted Allocation is Strictly Smaller than $1-1/e$
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: A well-known conjecture in online algorithms is that the (randomized) competitive ratio of online budgeted allocation is $1-1/e$. We refute this conjecture and show that every randomized online algorithm has competitive ratio at most $1 - 1/e - \varepsilon$ for a (small) absolute constant $\varepsilon > 0$.

Emerging Technologies.title: Analog and hybrid computing in the 21st century
Emerging Technologies.summary: Analog computers solve problems through physical representations of mathematical variables and relations, often using the dynamics of electronic circuits and their associated signals. Many analog computers directly represent nonlinear dynamical systems; they encode their solutions in the signals that they generate. Although most modern scientific computing relies on digital architectures with inherently discrete-valued representations and algorithmic approaches, the design constraints of such architectures increasingly limit both performance and energy efficiency. Analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints; they execute specific computations very efficiently by mapping them directly onto physical processes using smaller and simpler computing elements than the ones in digital architectures. In this article, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid (i.e., analog-digital) computing. We discuss how modern scientific computing workflows can leverage analog approaches in various applications, such as in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimization, and enabling more energy-efficient implementations of artificial intelligence.

Emerging Technologies.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
Emerging Technologies.summary: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

Emerging Technologies.title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity
Emerging Technologies.summary: Morphogenesis of diatom silica shells involves a sequence of topological transitions: initially separate ribs grow and branch, then merge through bridges, leaving a regular network of pores. Existing models based on diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion reproduce either branching or pore formation, but not both within a single framework. Here we propose a two-stage model of diffusion-driven morphogenesis with evolving connectivity. The model is formulated on a fixed finite element mesh with a density field on an active layer. Stage 1 reproduces dendritic growth, where a stimulus based on the local diffusive flux exceeds a threshold. Stage 2 uses an inverted stimulus, where high local flux suppresses precipitation, stabilizing pores between the dendrites. The update rules are analogous to sensitivity in density-based topology optimization and to strain energy density in bone remodeling. The model predicts distinct morphological regimes on each stage, controlled by the respective thresholds. For a reference calculation, the predicted pore network is regular, with approximately uniform spacing, and pores are absent near the domain edges, consistent with observations on diatom valves. The model provides a unified framework for describing both stages of silica morphogenesis and suggests a route for comparing computational predictions with cryo-electron tomography data.
Emerging Technologies.comment: Submitted to Applied Mathematical Modelling. Animation available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23808711

Emerging Technologies.title: Clinical-Protocol-Aware Cyber Resilience for Connected Clinical Technologies Under AI-Enabled Adversarial Conditions
Emerging Technologies.summary: Healthcare increasingly relies on connected medical devices, clinical information systems, cloud services, and distributed-care technologies, creating cybersecurity risks across clinical workflows. AI-enabled capabilities can accelerate vulnerability discovery and attack-path analysis, increasing the need to limit compromise propagation. This paper proposes a clinical-protocol-aware cyber-resilience framework based on bounded clinical micro-networks and controlled interconnections. The framework integrates clinical factors into cybersecurity design, management, and evaluation, covering prevention, containment, and incident response. A parameterized Monte Carlo simulation distinguishes technical cyber exposure from modeled clinical consequence. Experiments investigate architectural connectivity, adversarial capability, security controls, protocol dependency, risk alignment, communication directionality, lifecycle integration, and response timing. Under the simulation assumptions, connected architecture increases mean cyber exposure by 56.3% relative to segmented architecture, while combined prevention and containment reduce exposure by 60.1% relative to no controls. Increasing protocol dependency raises the modeled clinical-impact index from 1.021 to 7.567 without changing mean cyber exposure, demonstrating that technical exposure and clinical consequence can diverge. Risk-alignment experiments further indicate higher modeled clinical impact when greater technical risk corresponds to greater clinical significance. The findings support comparative architectural analysis, not calibrated estimates of real-world cyber risk, control effectiveness, or patient harm. The framework provides a clinical-context-aware approach to security-boundary design, control prioritization, and coordinated containment in connected healthcare environments.
Emerging Technologies.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Emerging Technologies.title: Matter that learns what matters
Emerging Technologies.summary: Can a material learn what deserves its attention? We show this in a model optical network, where action outcomes train a persistent record in each link. The record biases whether a source is consulted and sets how strongly it changes a stored answer, so useful sources gain attention and influence without being identified in advance. The network's experience thus shapes the information available for its future learning. Resonant readouts make this learning fragile: reinforcement can carry a record past resonance, where it persists but its influence weakens. We derive bounds within which relevant signals guide the answer, irrelevant signals are rejected and stored answers remain open to revision. These bounds guide a learning rule that limits reinforcement as records form; in simulations, it acquires useful records and keeps them functional. When relevance changes, an obsolete record can block its own replacement. A local state that strengthens negative writing after unsuccessful actions releases obsolete records and completes the learning sequence more often. A reduced stochastic model, calibrated retrospectively from local response statistics, accounts for changes in sequence completion across writing rules without fitting the aggregate success rates. How a memory is read should decide how it is written.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. Version v2 contains the links to Zenodo and a new subsection, ''Reduced stochastic model of the learning sequence.''

Emerging Technologies.title: Communication-Aware Qubit Placement and Automatic Node-Count Allocation for Distributed State-Vector Simulation
Emerging Technologies.summary: Quantum circuit simulation enables the execution of large-scale quantum algorithms by partitioning qubits across multiple computational nodes. However, an inefficient qubit placement leads to excessive inter-node communication, limiting performance and scalability. This work introduces a framework that computes a communication-aware qubit placement offline, minimizing data exchange among nodes, and selects, before circuit execution, the largest node count whose performance degradation stays below a user-defined threshold. The framework is integrated with the QuEST simulator. Evaluations on synthetic benchmarks and real-world QASMBench circuits show that optimized placements reduce communication and achieve runtime speedups of up to 2.3x over the identity placement, particularly in circuits with sparse, structured interactions. Our results show that qubit placement strongly affects the efficiency of distributed simulation and provide a practical, resource-scalable solution for quantum workload

Emerging Technologies.title: Input-dependent Neuromodulation Enhances Mixed-Signal Neuromorphic Hardware
Emerging Technologies.summary: Gating mechanisms allow a fixed neural network to adapt its computation to the current input by dynamically modulating its effective parameters. In the brain, neuromodulation uses this principle to move neural circuits between dynamical regimes, and deep learning exploits input-dependent gating, e.g., in gated recurrent networks and self-attention. Input-dependent modulation has also recently been shown to improve spiking neural networks, with particularly strong benefits in small, parameter-limited ones. This makes neuromodulation especially promising for neuromorphic processors at the edge, where area, memory and energy budgets constrain network size, while circuit physics limits parameter precision. Here we demonstrate input-dependent, within-trial neuromodulation of a spiking recurrent neural network on a mixed-signal neuromorphic processor. An off-chip modulator reads the on-chip network's input and activity and adjusts its population-level gains while the chip's analog circuits compute with the physics of the silicon. Neuromodulation raises binary spoken-digit classification accuracy by $+17.3 \pm 10.4$ percentage points, tested across five hardware network instantiations.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE ISCAS 2027

Emerging Technologies.title: ZenKO: Guided and Iterative Quantum-Classical Method for Molecular Electronic Structure using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
Emerging Technologies.summary: The electronic structure of molecules is foundational for scientific advancement, however determining it remains challenging due to the growth of the molecular Hilbert space with system size. Recent approaches address this by using quantum circuits to sample candidate configurations and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to compute the ground state. We propose ZenKO, a novel gradient-based, iterative SQD method that employs a hybrid quantum-classical approach. ZenKO decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement, enabling targeted subspace expansion and guided exploration. Our evaluation demonstrates that, across $H_2O$, $H_{10}$, and $N_2$ molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy compared to prior iterative methods, while significantly reducing classical cost.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 12 pages, 17 figures, Accepted at SC26: The International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, Chicago, IL, USA, November 15-20, 2026

Emerging Technologies.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
Emerging Technologies.summary: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

Graphics.title: Toolpath Overhang Optimization for the Large-Format 3D Printing of Bespoke Shapes
Graphics.summary: This paper presents a closed curve trimming algorithm for overhang optimization in large-format support-free 3D printing of bespoke manifold shapes. Large-format 3D printing enables efficient fabrication of complex, bespoke shapes. Because of the material properties and surface quality requirements, such shapes are typically printed without support structures and have to be designed as support-free. Most current methods of overhang optimization are limited to certain types of geometry and do not apply to bespoke shapes. Our method directly optimizes sliced toolpath curves with minimal geometric modification. Given an overhang limit, it ensures that all resulting toolpath curves are strictly within the overhang limit while preserving their orientation and preventing intersections. The algorithm is based on curve offsetting and trimming, and is applicable to closed toolpath curves that represent the boundaries of a solid volume.

Graphics.title: Piecewise CMC Segmentation for Fluidic Shaping
Graphics.summary: We present a novel mesh segmentation approach for the fabrication of 3D geometries using fluidic shaping. The physics of fluidic shaping gives rise to Constant Mean Curvature (CMC) surfaces due to interfacial tension between the polymer fluid used to shape the 3D structure and an immersion fluid of equal density. Our mesh segmentation algorithm partitions the mesh into a piecewise CMC surface, such that every segment is a CMC approximation to the target within a user specified tolerance. We run a CMC evolution procedure in the loop during segmentation to find physically stable CMC surfaces that can be reliably fabricated. We extract a wireframe scaffold from the seams of this segmentation and inject polymer fluid into the frame for curing. The structure cures as a single, continuous, isotropic volume, yielding nanometer scale roughness on the interior surface of each segment without the costly post-processing or smoothing that conventional state-of-the-art approaches require for comparable surface quality.

Graphics.title: SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid
Graphics.summary: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

Graphics.title: How to Simplify a Line Chart: A Taxonomy and Feature-Based Evaluation
Graphics.summary: Simplifying large or noisy time-series is often a prerequisite for producing interpretable line charts, yet existing methods vary widely in how they alter visual features such as trends, extrema, periodicity, curvature, roughness, and overall complexity. We introduce a feature-based taxonomy of line chart simplification that evaluates 19 commonly used algorithms across three families: Transformers, Reducers, and Aggregators. We also formalize 12 perceptually motivated, computationally defined visual features commonly used when analyzing time-series in line charts. We assess preservation using multiple similarity metrics per feature to capture different aspects of fidelity, yielding 21 distinct feature-preservation measurements. To capture the trade-off between fidelity and simplicity, we introduce a Feature--Complexity (FC) score that combines feature preservation with complexity. Our systematic evaluation on 80 datasets reveals distinct family-level patterns: Transformers such as Gaussian, Mean, and Median filters achieve A-mode grades on nearly all metrics but retain full temporal resolution; Reducers such as Douglas-Peucker and M4 receive predominantly D-F mode grades trading fidelity for a reduction in the number of rendered points; and Aggregators ASAP and PAA occupy a middle ground with primarily B-C mode grades. We further characterize the predictability of algorithm behavior across datasets: some methods produce consistent grades regardless of dataset type (Gaussian, Mean, Douglas-Peucker), while others exhibit high data-dependency, with performance varying substantially based on dataset characteristics (FPCS, ASAP). An interactive website supporting exploration of all evaluated techniques, datasets, and results is available at https://feature-taxonomy.vercel.app/.

Graphics.title: Frequency-Adaptive Gaussian Grids for Efficient Image Representation
Graphics.summary: Neural representation has emerged as a powerful tool to mitigate the demand for increasingly higher-resolution images. However, a fundamental trade-off remains between structured (e.g., feature grids, which offer spatial consistency) and unstructured (e.g., 2D Gaussians, which adaptively capture local variances) representations. This choice significantly affects how well an algorithm represents an image. Here, we present Gaussian-Grid, a hybrid neural representation that adaptively integrates structured and unstructured primitives. By dynamically partitioning computation between 2D Gaussian distributions and their attached multi-resolution feature grids based on the local frequency content, Gaussian-Grid automatically optimizes its architecture to match the underlying complexity of the target signal. We evaluate our approach using high-resolution natural images and demonstrate its applications as GPU-native dataset storage, showing $1.24$-$2.14\times$ decoding speed improvement and PCIe data traffic reduction of $23\times$-$176\times$ over JPEG + ZIP data archiving. The results show that Gaussian-Grid maintains small memory footprints while achieving high reconstruction fidelity across a variety of datasets.

Graphics.title: Altered Visual Hand Feedback in Virtual Reality: An Exploratory Study in Essential Tremor
Graphics.summary: Pathological tremor is the most prevalent movement disorder worldwide, characterized by involuntary muscular oscillations within a frequency of 3 to 12 Hz. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms that generate and modulate tremor are not yet understood, and treatments are usually insufficient. While it is known that visual feedback is an important afferent pathway, little is known about the impact of altering the hand's visual representation on tremor expression. With the development of immersive technologies, VR poses an excellent tool to study how alterations to the representation of the hands affect tremor. In this work, we study this through two complementary experiments. In the first one, we show that a consumer-level hand-tracking system substantially attenuates tremor-band movements without preventing successful task completion. In the second one, with eight patients with essential tremor, we observe task-dependent differences in physical tremor between VR and the real world, with several patients exhibiting lower tremor-band activity in both hand kinematics and muscle oscillations, particularly during reaching tasks. Our findings represent an initial step toward validating the use of VR as an experimental tool for the research and treatment of pathological tremor, while highlighting strong user- and task-dependent effects.

Multiagent Systems.title: Hybrid epidemic simulation framework coupling equation-based and individual-based models
Multiagent Systems.summary: Mass gathering events (MGEs) can create intense, short-lived transmission hotspots whose effects propagate through urban populations. Quantifying these effects requires linking fine-scale interactions during gatherings with epidemic transmission across metropolitan mobility networks. We developed a hybrid multiscale simulation framework coupling empirically derived individual-based contact networks for MGEs with a stochastic metapopulation susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered (SEIR) model. Using population and commuting data from Madrid, Spain, we investigated how event-related transmission affects epidemic dynamics and district-level invasion. Across the scenarios examined, MGEs increased epidemic peak incidence and accelerated epidemic progression, although the magnitude of these effects depended on event-specific contact patterns and background transmissibility. Dense contact patterns produced greater epidemic amplification, whereas measures reducing close-contact interactions weakened these effects. MGEs also advanced epidemic invasion across districts and increased the temporal synchronization of arrival times, producing a more synchronized metropolitan epidemic wave. The association between MGEs and earlier district-level invasion was partly explained by the size of the event-generated epidemic seed. The main patterns persisted across the epidemiological parameter ranges examined. The framework provides a multiscale approach for investigating how mass gathering management may influence metropolitan epidemic dynamics.
Multiagent Systems.comment: main text (10 pages, 9 figures), supplementary materials (11 pages, 10 figures, 4 tables)

Multiagent Systems.title: MafiaScope: Inspecting Multi-Agent Reasoning in Social Deduction Games
Multiagent Systems.summary: An LLM agent's public behaviour reveals little about its social reasoning: an agent that votes correctly may be guessing, and its public claims may differ from privately elicited assessments. We present MafiaScope, an open testbed that turns the social deduction game Mafia into a measurement instrument for multi-agent reasoning. After each public utterance, living agents privately answer configurable structured questions on copies of their available conversations. Probing is non-invasive with respect to the acting context: neither the questions nor the answers enter the histories used to continue the game. Role assessments are scored against roles known to the engine; second-order predictions are compared with other agents' reports. An interactive visualizer renders the assessment trajectories: impersonate mode focuses on one agent's information and reports, panels chart timeline-aligned accuracy and calibration, and counterfactual replay branches from saved states. An offline heuristic links shifts in collective suspicion to episodes for inspection. Experiments span multiple models, languages, and probing configurations; the demonstration presents episode inspection, calibration, probe-repeatability and probe/no-probe checks, and utterance-replacement replay. Code: https://github.com/karpovilia/mafiascope Demo: https://karpovilia.github.io/mafiascope Video: https://vimeo.com/1208920221

Multiagent Systems.title: Switchcraft: AI Model Router for Agentic Tool Calling
Multiagent Systems.summary: Agentic AI systems that invoke external tools are powerful but costly, leading developers to default to large models and overspend inference budgets. Existing model routers target chat responses or end-task success, not the correctness of the individual tool calls on which agent tasks depend; we present Switchcraft, the first (to the best of our knowledge) model router optimized for strict tool-call correctness in agentic workloads. We construct an evaluation framework on six function-calling benchmarks, holding one out entirely, and fine-tune a calibrated DistilBERT-based classifier, deployed inline under a latency budget, to select the lowest-cost model subject to correctness or abstain when none is likely to answer correctly. Switchcraft reaches 78.3% answer accuracy (86.4% when correct abstentions are credited) at 59% lower cost than the best individual model (75.6%), saving over $3,800 per million queries, and outperforms kNN, MIRT, heuristic, and random routers. On the held-out benchmark, it matches or exceeds every individual model at 5--7X lower cost than the strongest ones. We find two counter-intuitive results: larger models do not consistently outperform smaller ones on tool-use tasks, and nominally cheaper models can incur higher total cost due to token-intensive output.

Multiagent Systems.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
Multiagent Systems.summary: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.
Multiagent Systems.comment: First two authors contributed equally. Project Page: https://lingyunxiao18.github.io/ParallACT/

Multiagent Systems.title: Generalized Intention Modeling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Multiagent Systems.summary: Modeling an opponent's intent is critical for effective decision-making in non-cooperative, competitive, and general-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning. Existing opponent modeling methods encode intent using an embedding derived from episode information chosen a priori, such as the opponent's next action or a future environment state, and use this to guide the ego-agent's behavior. These approaches assume that the chosen information is universally representative of intent; however, we show empirically that this is not the case as intentions are often task- and environment-dependent. To address this, we introduce a task-adaptive opponent modeling framework that learns a performance-driven mixture of multiple intent representations. We further introduce a new intention representation that maximizes mutual information with the ego-agent's future returns, thereby capturing opponent information that is most directly relevant to performance. Our approach consistently matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse tasks and yields insights into when and why different opponent modeling strategies succeed.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Multiagent Systems.title: Self-Building Labs
Multiagent Systems.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still requires extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

Multiagent Systems.title: Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
Multiagent Systems.summary: Motivated by a broad literature in psychology, organizational behavior, and matching markets, we introduce strategic tanking: an agent deliberately makes themselves less attractive to selected potential partners in order to improve their eventual assignment. Unlike traditional manipulation in stable matching, a tanker does not misreport whom they prefer; instead, they influence how others rank them. We show that tanking has a striking connection to classical preference manipulation. Cutoff tanking, in which an agent tanks with every potential partner below a chosen threshold, has exactly the same effect on the stable set as truncating one's own preference list at that threshold. Thus an agent can reproduce the power of a classical truncation while leaving their own preferences unchanged and every match acceptable. Arbitrary tanking, however, can go substantially further: under proposer-deferred acceptance, tanking equilibria can lie outside the sincere stable set. More broadly, whenever the sincere stable set contains multiple matchings, profitable strategic behavior remains available through either traditional preference manipulation or tanking, even when one side is restricted to honestly reporting their own preferences.

Multiagent Systems.title: A Cross-Layered Multi-Drone Coordination for Medical Supply Delivery during Disaster Response Management
Multiagent Systems.summary: Autonomous drone fleets have potential in medical supply delivery during disaster incident response. However, coordinating multiple drones in such settings introduces compounding challenges: dynamic hazards such as wind, obstacles, and intermittent connectivity, constrained energy budgets, and the need to serve patients fairly under strict deadlines and triage-based priority. We present CEDA, a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) Double Deep Q-Network algorithm augmented with a QMIX-style monotonic mixing network for cooperative multi-drone medical delivery, designed to jointly optimize triage-aware routing, multi-agent coordination, and energy-efficient navigation under dynamic uncertainty. CEDA introduces a Priority-Preserving Fair Scheduling strategy, in which a structured reward function encodes triage priority weights, outcome-level fairness and priority-ordering rewards, and complementary shaping mechanisms that discourage systematic starvation. We evaluate CEDA in a simulated grid environment with five drones serving up to fifty patients, featuring dynamic hazard zones, stochastic action failures, and dynamically spawning patients across three triage levels, and in PX4 software-in-the-loop (SITL) validation using five X500 quadrotors controlled via MAVSDK. Simulation results show that CEDA delivers over 95\% of spawned patients, reduces obstacle collisions by over 95\% across training, and achieves a weighted triage efficiency exceeding 0.90 alongside a Jain's Fairness Index of approximately 1.0 across triage classes. CEDA preserves clinical priority ordering, with Critical patients receiving the fastest response times, while achieving low and comparable mortality across all triage classes. PX4 SITL validation further shows that the learned policy retains its triage-aware behavior under continuous simulated flight and delayed-action conditions.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables

Multiagent Systems.title: Adaptive Coverage Algorithms for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks in Dynamic Worlds
Multiagent Systems.summary: This paper extends an existing framework for the coordination of mobile agents in unknown worlds, by considering the possibility of dynamic instability. In the original problem, known as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) (arXiv:2512.09495), the multi-agent system must establish a communication network which completely covers an initially unknown constrained space. However, the POCGAGP fails to account for the unpredictability often seen in real-world deployment. To address this, the dynamic case (DPOCGAGP) introduces two settings which can influence the mobile network during deployment: Agent Loss and World Change, which represent dynamic changes to the world. Within this study, we present advancements to two state-of-the-art algorithms, the Centralized Agent-Directed Exploration for Network Coverage (CADENCE), and its decentralized analogue, DADENCE, to provide solutions in these cases. We then compare their performance against another state-of-the-art benchmark algorithm, and show that the adapted algorithms outperform across our benchmark test set, which comprises over 4500 test cases of varied size and structure.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)

Multiagent Systems.title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
Multiagent Systems.summary: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

Multiagent Systems.title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
Multiagent Systems.summary: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.

Multiagent Systems.title: Denoising Multirobot Trajectories
Multiagent Systems.summary: Multi-robot trajectory planning is a fundamental problem in multi-robot coordination but remains computationally challenging due to its nonconvex, multimodal, and high-dimensional nature. This work builds upon D4orm, a dynamics-aware diffusion-denoising framework, and develops a family of planning architectures for diverse operational requirements. Unlike conventional numerical optimization methods, D4orm employs sampling-based optimization to generate solution trajectories through massively parallel sampling, leveraging modern computing architectures such as GPUs. Its diffusion-denoising structure iteratively optimizes deformations to candidate control trajectories, providing an efficient and versatile paradigm for generating kinodynamically feasible and conflict-free trajectories. Using D4orm as the building block for advanced planners, we present a decoupled planner for improved scalability, an online receding-horizon planner with feedback control, and a distributed planner for resource-constrained settings. Evaluations with differential-drive and holonomic robots in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that D4orm-based approaches find high-quality solutions faster and more reliably than other sampling-based optimization methods, such as MPPI, as well as a learned diffusion-model-based method. We further demonstrate zero-shot deployment on ten real quadrotors with obstacles, large-scale deconfliction with 100 simulated robots, and fully onboard distributed `lifelong' operation with six ground robots. Overall, these results establish diffusion denoising as a scalable and reliable framework for multi-robot coordination. Code and video: https://github.com/proroklab/d4orm
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO) 2026

Multiagent Systems.title: ORION: An Outcome-Driven LLM Advisor for RL-Based Multi-Domain 6G Slice Placement
Multiagent Systems.summary: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted at IEEE MobiWac 2026

Multiagent Systems.title: Distributed Grid Search for Hyperparameter Tuning
Multiagent Systems.summary: The performance of many distributed optimization algorithms over peer-to-peer networks strongly depends on the choice of their hyperparameters. However, existing selection rules often require global quantities, yield conservative choices, or are tied to specific algorithms and hyperparameters. We propose Distributed Grid Search (D-GS), a consensus-based search method that evaluates and selects hyperparameter configurations across the network, requiring only the ability to run the tuned algorithm and evaluate local gradients. We also propose a zoom-in variant, Distributed Zoom Grid Search (D-ZGS), which improves empirical performance at a reduced cost. We prove that both methods terminate in finite time with all agents holding the same hyperparameter configuration, and quantify the (sub)optimality of this configuration. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression show that D-GS closely matches a centralized reference and that tuning and deployment cost a fraction of deploying algorithms with hyperparameters tuned using theoretical results.

Multiagent Systems.title: Anchor and Perturb: Lazy Agent Remediation by Exploration Injection
Multiagent Systems.summary: Anchor and Perturb (AnP) is a lightweight framework that resolves multi-agent coordination failures by decoupling exploratory variance injection from recurrent manifold stability. Existing remediation strategies predominantly alter mixing network architectures or enforce simultaneous exploration across the collective, which inevitably precipitates severe temporal-difference penalties in non-monotonic reward spaces. Specifically, AnP isolates underperforming lazy agents and injects an asymmetric exploratory pulse into targeted coordinates whilst anchoring converged teammates to nominal greedy exploitation.
